Home Depot Taps Longtime Exec for CEO as Manufacturer Faces ‘Frozen Housing Market’

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (566 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that home Depot COO Richard McPhail was revealed as the tech giant's fresh CEO on Tuesday, ahead of the home improvement giant's third-quarter earnings call.
  • In a recent development, mcPhail is taking the reins from Ted Decker, who will stay on as chairman.
  • McPhail has been with Home Depot since 2005 and previously served as executive vice president and chief financial officer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that home Depot COO Richard McPhail was revealed as the tech giant's fresh CEO on Tuesday, ahead of the home improvement giant's third-quarter earnings call. McPhail will take over on Nov. 23.

In a recent development, mcPhail is taking the reins from Ted Decker, who will stay on as chairman. Decker stepped into the role in 2022.

McPhail has been with Home Depot since 2005 and previously served as executive vice president and chief financial officer.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, Ann-Marie Campbell was named president and chief operating officer. Campbell began her career with the retailer 41 years ago, as a sales associate and most recently served as an executive vice president in charge of U.S. stores as well as Home Depot Canada, Home Depot Mexico, and Pro sales and services.

On Tuesday, during its third-quarter earnings call, the company reported better than expected quarterly revenue of $43.4 billion, up 4.9% from a year ago.

In remarks during the call, McPhail said Home Depot is “continuing to gain market share in a pressured housing market.".

During the firm's second-quarter earnings call in August, McPhail spoke of the "consumer uncertainty" around the housing market.

"While consumer uncertainty and housing affordability continue to pressure demand for larger home improvement projects, we remain focused on what we can control, our strategy of driving our core and culture, delivering a frictionless, interconnected experience, and winning the pro," he said.

Recent findings suggest that when asked during the call whether higher interest rates were impacting the housing market, McPhail opined that it was actually a lack of housing inventory that was creating a sluggish market. At the time of the second-quarter calls, rates were 6.67% but have since climbed to 7.21%.

"With respect to rates, as we have remarked over the past few years, housing turnover, just as one point in the economy that we watch, has been at historical lows," he said. "It has never been lower as a percentage of the housing stock. Every time we have seen it hit the sort of 3% of the housing stock changing hands, over history, it has always bounced up relatively promptly. We have seen housing turnover at these low levels for four years now. I do not think that we have seen much volatility from the recent increase in rates. We do know that when we see step downs, we begin to see a little bit of life come into housing, but there is just no sign of an inflection point at this moment.".

Following that meeting, McPhail acknowledged the "frozen housing market" in a conversation with CNBC.

“We continue to operate in what I call ‘frozen housing market conditions,’ but we also know that we’re taking share and that we’re serving our customers better every day,” he said. “It’s a reflection of the continued investment we’ve made and the focus on executing our strategy.”.

#30009. Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1280 w)

Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1280 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A surprising new study has found that people who are overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia tend to live longer than those who have a normal body weight.
  • In a recent development, researchers from Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and NYU School of Global Public Health found that body weight at the time of diagnosis may provide key clues about how long someone with dementia is likely to live.
  • Sources indicate that the results are particularly intriguing because obesity is well established as a risk factor for several serious health problems, including heart disease and diabetes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A surprising new study has found that people who are overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia tend to live longer than those who have a normal body weight. The findings challenge expectations about the relationship between weight and health, suggesting that carrying extra weight may be associated with an unexpected survival advantage after dementia develops.

In a recent development, researchers from Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and NYU School of Global Public Health found that body weight at the time of diagnosis may provide key clues about how long someone with dementia is likely to live. Their findings, published in the Journal of Alzheimer's Disease, also highlight the importance of proper nutrition for people living with the condition.

Sources indicate that the results are particularly intriguing because obesity is well established as a risk factor for several serious health problems, including heart disease and diabetes. Being overweight or obese during middle age is also associated with a greater likelihood of developing dementia later in life. However, previous research has suggested that the relationship may reverse once dementia has developed, with higher body weight linked to better survival.

Sources indicate that "Because this finding is somewhat counterintuitive, an vital question is whether it could simply be an artifact of bias. Our analyses suggest that the major sources of bias we examined do not explain the survival advantage associated with higher weight," stated corresponding author Yuan Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of Sociomedical Sciences at Columbia Mailman and in the Butler Columbia Aging Center.

Obesity Linked to Up to 27% Lower Risk of Death.

The researchers found substantial differences in survival based on body weight at the time of dementia diagnosis. Compared with individuals in the normal weight range, those who were overweight or obese had a significantly lower risk of death, even after the researchers accounted for smoking, existing medical conditions, and demographic characteristics.

Industry observers note that people classified as overweight (body mass index of 25 to 29.9) had a 16 percent lower risk of death. Those with class 1 obesity (BMI of 30 to 34.9) had an even larger reduction of 27 percent, while individuals with class 2 and 3 obesity (BMI equal to or greater than 35) had a 22 percent lower risk.

Despite these striking differences, the researchers caution that the findings should not be interpreted as a recommendation for people with dementia to gain weight.

"This doesn't mean that patients with dementia should attempt to become overweight or obese, as our study was not designed to test that question. But our findings do suggest that weight status may serve as a useful prognostic signal for survival at the time of dementia diagnosis. They also support the notion that nutrition is a key factor in the health and survival of people with dementia," stated Virginia Chang, associate professor of Social and Behavioral Sciences at NYU School of Global Public Health and the study's first author.

Tracking Weight and Dementia Over 24 Years.

To investigate the connection, Zhang, Chang, and their colleagues examined information from the Health and Retirement Study, a nationally representative research project that follows Americans ages 51 and older.

The team analyzed records collected between 1998 and 2022, focusing on 4,523 participants who did not have dementia when they entered the study but subsequently developed the condition.

Because the data covered such a long period, the researchers could examine how participants' weight changed in the years leading up to their diagnosis. They could also determine their weight when dementia was identified and track their survival afterward.

In a recent development, this extended timeline was especially notable because scientists have questioned whether the apparent benefit of higher body weight is genuine or simply reflects misleading patterns in the data. One possibility is that having additional fat or muscle gives patients resources that help them withstand the physical effects of dementia. Another is that the association arises from factors that earlier studies did not adequately consider.

Could Weight Loss Explain the Dementia Paradox?

One major concern involves weight loss that occurs before dementia becomes clinically apparent.

Earlier research by Zhang and Chang found that people can begin losing weight as much as 10 years before a dementia diagnosis, with the decline becoming more pronounced as the disease approaches.

It has been revealed that this creates a potential problem for studies that measure weight only at the time dementia is diagnosed. Some individuals classified as having a normal weight may previously have been heavier and lost weight because of the developing disease. If those individuals are already experiencing more advanced illness, they may face a greater risk of death, making higher body weight appear beneficial by comparison.

In a recent development, the researchers also considered other possible distortions. Restricting an analysis to people who develop dementia can create misleading relationships between obesity and mortality, even when the underlying connection is more complicated.

Another concern is known as "survivor" bias. Since people with obesity face an increased risk of dying from certain illnesses before reaching the age when dementia typically develops, those who survive long enough to receive a dementia diagnosis may represent an unusually healthy group.

In a recent development, to determine whether these factors explained the findings, the team performed additional analyses designed to evaluate several potential sources of bias. The results indicated that the biases they examined were unlikely to be major drivers of the observed connection between higher weight and lower mortality.

Why Extra Weight Might Help People With Dementia.

Although the precise explanation remains unknown, the researchers identified several biological reasons why additional body weight could be advantageous for someone already living with dementia.

One possibility involves the body's energy reserves. People with more stored fat or greater muscle mass may be better equipped to withstand periods of poor nutrition and the physical deterioration that can accompany the disease.

Recent findings suggest that dementia can interfere with eating in several ways. Changes in brain function may reduce appetite or motivation to eat, while some patients experience increased energy needs or gradually lose the ability to feed themselves. Over time, these problems can contribute to significant weight loss, muscle wasting, and declining health.

"Nutrition can be a massive problem for people with dementia," said Chang. "They may experience wasting and an inability to eat, which can be due to changes in the brain's central drive, leading to loss of appetite and initiative, increased energy expenditure, and difficulties feeding themselves.".

Having additional energy stores or muscle tissue could potentially help patients cope with these challenges, although the study did not establish that these factors directly explain the survival differences.

The researchers emphasize that crucial questions remain unanswered. Even after examining multiple potential biases and identifying plausible biological explanations, they cannot say for certain why overweight and obese participants experienced lower mortality.

Nevertheless, Zhang and Chang believe that weight at the time of a dementia diagnosis could provide valuable information about a patient's likely survival. The results also reinforce the importance of recognizing and addressing nutritional problems in people with dementia.

Additional study authors include Eleanor Hayes-Larson of the University of Southern California and Hui Zheng of the University of Toronto.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health (grant numbers R00AG070274, R00AG075317).

Heidi Overton’s FDA nomination pulled by White House

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Heidi Overton’s FDA nomination pulled by White House" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The White House pulled the nomination for Heidi Overton, M.D., Ph.D., to lead the FDA just hours before the Senate was scheduled to vote on her confirmation.

The move hardly comes as a surprise after Overton’s confirmation hearing before the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee drew contention.

According to recent reports, the news was first reported by Axios on Tuesday evening. The White House confirmed the news to Fierce the following morning.

In September, the HELP committee questioned Overton in a hearing marked by tightrope-walking on complications like vaccines, abortions, flavored vapes and whether or not President Donald Trump is capable of being wrong.

Overton conceded multiple times during the hearing that vaccines approved by the FDA, as well as the “abortion pill” mifepristone, are safe and effective. But she stopped short of admitting that Trump has been wrong when dispensing medical information out of line with what scientific evidence reveals.

Recent findings suggest that overton’s nomination faced mounting pushback and uncertainty from senators ahead of a planned HELP Committee vote on Nov. 18. Fierce reached out to Sen. Ed Markey, the veteran Democratic lawmaker from Massachusetts, ahead of the vote, and he told Fierce that he would “vote against her nomination, and I urge my colleagues to do the same.”.

“The FDA needs a leader who will stand up for science and for our kids’ safety, not one who stood by while both were undermined,” he added.

Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who chairs the Senate health committee, and other Republicans had also raised questions about Overton's nomination.

As support for Overton looked thin, Republicans were discussing Sen. Roger Marshall, a Kansas Republican, as a potential replacement, Semafor reported today.

Robert Steinbrook, M.D., health research group director for Public Citizen, commented today urging the HELP committee to reject Overton’s nomination: “The FDA needs a strong commissioner who stands for science and the integrity of the agency,” Steinbrook remarked. “Overton is the wrong choice for FDA Commissioner and has done nothing to dispel the well-founded reasons to oppose her candidacy.”.

Analysts from Citi shared that the White House’s decision to pull the nomination has a negative impact on biopharma, “extending uncertainty around permanent agency leadership.”.

“We view the withdrawal as a modest sentiment negative, but not a material near-term change to the regulatory environment facing most drug and biologics sponsors,” the analysts mentioned in the note.

Recent findings suggest that the withdrawal of Overton's nomination leaves a gap at an FDA that has already faced significant upheaval. The White House only shifted its focus to Overton in August, after the agency had spent three months without a permanent leader.

Since former FDA commissioner Marty Makary, M.D., departed the agency in May, Kyle Diamantas, who hails from the agency’s food regulation division, has been at the helm in an interim capacity.

#30004. Latest Update: Even occasional marijuana use linked to 40% higher odds of stroke

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1388 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Even occasional marijuana use linked to 40% higher odds of stroke

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1388 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that newly introduced preliminary research involving more than 440,000 American adults has uncovered a concerning association between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease, particularly stroke.
  • Industry observers note that the research, presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, found that the association was not limited to people who frequently used cannabis.
  • Scientific Sessions 2026 took place November 6 through 9 in Chicago, bringing together cardiovascular researchers and healthcare professionals from around the world to share scientific discoveries, clinical advances, and emerging evidence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that newly introduced preliminary research involving more than 440,000 American adults has uncovered a concerning association between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease, particularly stroke. The findings suggest that even occasional marijuana use may be linked to higher odds of cardiovascular problems, raising new questions about the health effects of a substance that is becoming increasingly common across the United States.

Industry observers note that the research, presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, found that the association was not limited to people who frequently used cannabis. It also appeared across different methods of consumption (smoked or edible, etc.). Researchers emphasized that cannabis use should be considered when discussing heart health and stroke prevention.

Scientific Sessions 2026 took place November 6 through 9 in Chicago, bringing together cardiovascular researchers and healthcare professionals from around the world to share scientific discoveries, clinical advances, and emerging evidence.

Cannabis refers to the plant itself, while marijuana is a commonly used term for cannabis products containing enough THC to produce psychoactive effects.

Marijuana Use Is Rising Across the United States.

"Previous research has indicated that cannabis use is rapidly increasing in the United States, with 1 in 6 adults in 2024 reporting having used it within the last month, up from 1 in 10 in 2020 -- a 51% increase," remarked study author Aabha Divya, M.B.B.S., M.Ch., an assistant professor in the division of cardiothoracic surgery at the Tulane University School of Medicine in Fresh Orleans.

Recent findings suggest that earlier research conducted between 2016 and 2020 had already identified associations between cannabis consumption and unfavorable cardiovascular outcomes. Those findings also suggested that using cannabis more frequently during a given month was connected to greater cardiovascular risk.

However, the evidence has not always been consistent. With recreational marijuana becoming legal in more places and cannabis products increasingly available, Divya and colleagues wanted to investigate these possible health effects in a larger population.

"We wanted to expand on this earlier work because cannabis use has become increasingly common in the United States, as recreational legalization and commercial availability of various products with cannabis have also expanded. Previous studies have raised concerns about possible cardiovascular effects; however, the results have not been consistent," Divya noted.

The researchers examined information collected through the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS), a large telephone survey of American adults. They combined responses from jurisdictions that collected information about cannabis consumption between 2020 and 2024.

Participants answered questions about their marijuana use and whether a healthcare professional had ever diagnosed them with cardiovascular conditions, including a heart attack, stroke, or coronary heart disease.

Even Occasional Marijuana Use Was Linked to Higher Stroke Odds.

One of the most striking findings was that infrequent cannabis use was associated with cardiovascular problems. In fact, the researchers did not find the steady increase in cardiovascular risk with more frequent use that they had expected.

The analysis revealed several important associations:.

These findings were unexpected because the relationship between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease did not consistently become stronger as consumption increased.

"We were surprised to find that the link between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease was not straightforward. We expected that the chances of heart disease would gradually rise as people used cannabis more often, but that wasn't the case. Both low-use and heavy-use groups had higher odds of developing heart disease," Divya said.

Although the study cannot establish that marijuana directly causes strokes or other cardiovascular conditions, the findings suggest that occasional consumption should not automatically be considered free of potential cardiovascular concerns.

"As cannabis use becomes more common, it is increasingly notable that people and their healthcare professionals include it in conversations about cardiovascular health, just as they discuss tobacco, alcohol and other commonly used substances," she added.

Experts Urge Greater Attention to Cannabis and Heart Health.

It has been revealed that robert L. Page II, Pharm.D., M.S.P.H., FAHA, who led the writing group responsible for the American Heart Association's 2020 cannabis scientific statement, said the findings add to growing concerns about marijuana's possible cardiovascular effects.

One challenge in evaluating those effects is that many cannabis users also smoke tobacco. Because tobacco is already an established cardiovascular risk factor, separating its effects from those of cannabis can be difficult.

Page, who was not involved in the research, explained why the new findings deserve attention.

Sources indicate that "Unfortunately, many patients who use cannabis may also smoke tobacco, which completely clouds the issue when addressing atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk. In patients who use both, cannabis has always been considered an innocent bystander; however, this is not the case. This is the second observational study to suggest that cannabis exposure (without tobacco smoking) may be a potential risk factor for developing cardiovascular disease. Overall, cannabis is beginning to emerge as a major contributor to premature heart disease in young and older adults, which can lead to serious cardiovascular events. To this end, clinicians should be addressing cannabis use with their patients as they would tobacco use when considering the risk of cardiovascular disease.".

Page is a professor in the department of clinical pharmacy and the department of physical medicine/rehabilitation at the University of Colorado Skaggs School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences in Aurora, Colorado.

How Researchers Studied Nearly Half a Million Americans.

It has been revealed that the analysis included 442,906 adults living in the United States (average age of 49 years; approximately half women). Their responses came from telephone surveys conducted through the BRFSS.

Researchers used survey information collected from 2020 through 2024, focusing on states that had included an optional marijuana questionnaire. Between 16 and 24 states participated in this portion of the survey each year, meaning the analysis did not represent every state.

Industry observers note that participants reported how many days they had consumed cannabis during the preceding month. The questions covered multiple ways of using marijuana (smoking, vaping or ingesting gummies or other cannabis-containing foods).

The researchers divided participants into four categories based on their reported use:.

Participants also indicated whether they had ever received a diagnosis of heart attack, heart disease, heart-related chest pain, or stroke.

To better distinguish the association with cannabis from other potential explanations, the researchers accounted for numerous established cardiovascular risk factors. These included demographic characteristics, tobacco smoking, alcohol consumption, obesity, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, physical inactivity, education, and income.

Why the Findings Do Not Prove Marijuana Causes Strokes.

Despite the large number of participants, the study has several limitations that affect how its findings should be interpreted.

According to recent reports, first, the analysis examined associations between reported cannabis use and previously diagnosed cardiovascular conditions at a single point in time. This means researchers could not determine whether marijuana use preceded the cardiovascular problems or whether it directly contributed to them.

It has been revealed that the information also depended on participants accurately recalling and reporting their cannabis consumption and medical histories (making them subject to potential errors in memory). Such reports may not always reflect actual patterns of use or diagnoses.

Sources indicate that another limitation was the lack of information about the strength of the cannabis products participants consumed or the quantities they used. Without those details, the researchers could not evaluate whether THC potency or the amount consumed influenced the observed associations.

The researchers also acknowledged that some participants may have reduced or discontinued cannabis consumption after being diagnosed with cardiovascular disease. As a result, the group reporting no cannabis use in the previous month may have included former users.

Industry observers note that these uncertainties make it difficult to draw firm conclusions about how consumption frequency affects cardiovascular health. Nevertheless, the findings add to growing evidence that cannabis use deserves closer examination as a possible factor in heart disease and stroke.

As marijuana becomes more widely available and its use continues to increase, researchers and healthcare professionals are emphasizing the importance of discussing cannabis alongside other substances that may affect cardiovascular health.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The two-bedroom, two-bathroom abode spans about 2,000 square feet—and decades of cultural history.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Upper West Side home of late film critic Rex Reed in the landmark building, The Dakota—where he lived for nearly 60 years—has hit the market, with an asking price just under $6 million.

The two-bedroom, two-bathroom abode spans about 2,000 square feet—and decades of cultural history.

Proceeds from the sale of the $5.99 million residence—as well as an upcoming estate auction—will fund the Rex Reed Foundation, an organization that seeks to uplift storytelling initiatives.

“Residence 86 at the Dakota is an oversized, high-floor corner two-bedroom made for serious entertaining,” listing agent Philip McCarthy of Sotheby’s International Realty tells Realtor.com®.

It has been revealed that the dwelling has certainly been used for exactly that. According to the Latest York Times, Reed hosted guests including Hollywood legends Lauren Bacall, Boris Karloff, and Truman Capote.

“He entertained a lot in his heyday, when he was hitting his stride in the late ‘60s and ‘70s,” Reed’s friend, Eric Baker, told the publication, noting that the parties had slowed in the last 15 years.

It has been revealed that reed—who passed in his home at 87, after a brief illness—snapped up the apartment in 1969 for just $30,000. Over the years, he would fill the home with curated antiques, artwork, and fascinating furnishings, despite having very few belongings in the beginning.

In a 2018 Fresh York Times interview, the journalist recalled moving in with “an A.&.P shopping cart, some books, and whatever I could drag over from my little walk-up on 73rd street” Reportedly, he had long dreamt of living in the iconic building, as it was where “Rosemary’s Baby” was filmed.

According to the listing, the building is the “oldest surviving luxury apartment building in Fresh York City.”.

“Apartments here rarely come to market, and a sale from a single owner after nearly six decades is rarer still,” the listing adds.

Reed clearly understood the gem he was sitting on, apparently turning down “The Phantom of the Opera” composer Andrew Lloyd Webber’s $8 million offer for the residence.

“I spent a lot of time getting this apartment just the way I wanted it, and I wouldn’t want to start over now,” Reed told The Observer at the time.

Although the home has been repainted and staged to sell, McCarthy told the New York Times that some of the writer’s “personal belongings were mixed in.”.

Still donning its original prewar layout, the unit makes an elegant first impression with a large formal gallery leading way to a generously sized living room and formal dining room, equipped with a dry bar and pantry.

The primary bedroom has an en suite bathroom, ample closet space, and a windowed nook well-suited for a home office or an idyllic reading spot.

The secondary bedroom, which Reed used as an office, also boasts an en suite, and has ample wardrobe storage, too. A full wall of built-in shelving once hosted his impressive media collection.

With high ceilings and north and west-facing windows that sit “well above the low-rise buildings” neighboring the Dakota, the stately residence is brimming with character.

Original architectural details—such as Regency doors and crown moldings—can still be found throughout the home.

Recent findings suggest that built in 1884, the Dakota sits on Central Park West and was designed by Henry J. Hardenbergh—who also completed the Plaza Hotel.

According to recent reports, the building includes a gated porte-cochère entrance, which leads to a central courtyard with original, restored fountains. The facade underwent a full restoration in 2017.

The Dakota’s monthly maintenance fee is $8,842, which provides access to “service, privacy, and security,” thanks to the dedicated resident manager, experienced concierge, doorman, and engineering and maintenance staff members.

Sources indicate that the building also has a state-of-the art fitness center, additional storage, and auxiliary laundry. The listing states that pets and pieds-à-terre are allowed, and buyers are permitted to finance up to 50%.

She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1253 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A customer buys a token on a U.S.
  • Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all.
  • Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

In a recent development, A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app demonstrates the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions.".

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

It has been revealed that for the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

It has been revealed that the CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control.".

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:.

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

According to recent reports, the SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

In a recent development, under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there.".

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks shows where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

It has been revealed that the CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Industry observers note that exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

HLTH 2026: How Whoop aims to play a bigger role in healthcare

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
HLTH 2026: How Whoop aims to play a bigger role in healthcare" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

LAS VEGAS—Whoop gained traction as a performance wearable used by elite athletes, professional teams and Olympians to track physiological strain and sleep.

It has been revealed that the company has evolved into a broader clinical and digital health platform that layers medical-grade hardware, blood diagnostics, electronic health record (EHR) syncing, and physician care on top of its continuous biometric tracking. The company's FDA-cleared ECG detects signs of atrial fibrillation and allows members to share results with their healthcare provider.

According to recent reports, whoop is a screenless, wrist-worn device that measures strain, recovery and sleep 24/7, paired with Whoop Coach, an AI-powered, in-app health and fitness assistant. The organization expanded its Advanced Labs testing—combining Quest blood testing, clinician reviews and AI insights—to non-members, alongside integrating Grail's multi-cancer early detection test. Whoop partners with health platform HealthEx to let people connect their medical records directly to the Whoop app, combining medical history with biometric data. A feature rolled out earlier this year lets Whoop members directly connect with clinicians through the app, including live, on-demand video consultations.

The company has raised over $900 million to date, including a $575 million series G round in March, pushing its valuation to $10 billion. Whoop told Bloomberg it aims to hire 600 people this year, a roughly 75% boost to its headcount, as it works to further integrate AI into its health and wellness monitoring tools and to expand internationally. The company is on track for an initial public offering in 18 months, executives told Bloomberg in August.

Sources indicate that the firm is positioning itself as a continuous health monitor that goes beyond fitness tracking. The device's 24/7 physiological data can function almost like an ongoing health check, becoming a bridge between everyday health and medical care, Will Ahmed, founder and CEO of Whoop, said during an on-stage interview at HLTH on Tuesday.

Ahmed argued that the conventional annual medical physical is "frozen in time.".

It has been revealed that "The reality is wearing a continuous health monitor like Whoop that should be a 24/7 annual checkup. That's how it should function from a data standpoint," he stated during a fireside chat with Michael Phelps, U.S. former competitive swimmer, who is the most decorated Olympian in history with 23 gold medals, and also a Whoop customer since 2015.

"Then there will be alerts when something is really wrong, and particularly as we combine these different data sources together, again, 24/7 physiological data, blood tests, medical records, how you're feeling and contextual cues. When we have all this information in one place, and now we've got 3.5 million members, about to be 4 million members, it's just amazing the insights that you can pull together from that. And so you can start to predict that someone may need to get a cancer screening, or may actually have a real heart problem," he stated.

In a recent development, whoop can pull together biometric data, labs, medical records and information to establish a baseline for an individual, recognize meaningful changes and recommend an action. By combining continuous monitoring with information such as blood tests, the manufacturer hopes to help consumers piece together health signals and determine when they may need care, Ahmed noted.

For Phelps, Whoop has shifted from being about maximizing elite athletic performance to helping him manage his health, energy and recovery around everyday life and longevity, he told the audience.

"For me, for 20-plus years, I've been trying to chase time, and now I'm just trying to be the healthiest person that I can be," Phelps remarked. "For me, the data that I get every single day, if my body isn't 100% or I'm not full go, then I take a step back and I tone down my workout. When I'm talking to my trainer, I'm taking it down a little bit, so I have enough energy and I have what I need to be a good dad, to be a good husband, to be a good worker, hard worker, whatever it is, just to be a good person.".

In a recent development, whoop sees opportunities to turn deviations from an individual's baseline into actionable signals. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Phelps said his Whoop device signaled that his temperature, respiratory rate and HRV changed, but he noted that the real benefit was that Whoop knew what normal looked like for him.

Using biometric data to recognize signals in a person's health can have broader implications, Ahmed noted, citing examples where members identified potentially serious health problems after noticing significant changes in their physiological data.

"We're just starting to see all of these different maps presenting themselves, and it's very empowering. We're excited about the role that we can play with the broader health ecosystem," Ahmed mentioned.

Ahmed stated Whoop's high user engagement and continuous monitoring can fill gaps between doctors' visits and provide clinically relevant information to care teams.

"I do believe that technology like Whoop can make the whole system much more efficient and also make a doctor's life easier if we do our jobs properly, which is again to say, how do you take all this information that's being collected about a patient or a consumer and how do you simplify it to the one, two, or three questions that a doctor might actually want to know the answer to before you show up to their office?" he said.

Ahmed sees the AI coach evolving into a personal health companion sitting on top of a longitudinal health record.

"That's another area that we're really excited about, where this idea that you can have a conversation with Whoop or what feels like this entity that sits on top of your data, and all of a sudden you feel like you have a health companion, and yes, you've got 24/7 physiological data from sensors, but you can also now have your medical records. You can also now have your blood tests. There are all sorts of conversational cues. 'How are you feeling today?' 'Did you drink alcohol last night?' Were you traveling?' You put all that information together, all that data in one place, and the insights are quite profound," he said.

Partnerships with other digital health companies and acquisitions help Whoop broaden the platform, he noted.

"We like to think about it from the consumer's vantage point first, which is to say, if you're an individual, if you're a consumer, what is data that you want on your body or you need on your body, and that may be data that's being collected somewhere else, in which case, we feel like there could be an opportunity for a partnership," Ahmed said, adding, "We're also comfortable now acquiring technology and acquiring different innovations, which has become more of a muscle that we've built over the last 12 months.".

Whoop believes its biggest strategic advantage is the consumer relationship.

Members open the app roughly eight times a day and wear the device nearly 23 hours a day.

"There are so many of us who have been in health tech where we would die for that kind of engagement, and I think that's something we're always striving for because we're an industry that was never built with the consumer in the center," mentioned Lynne O'Keefe, founder and manager partner of Define Ventures, who moderated the on-stage interview.

The company is strategically expanding into an older, more medical population. Whoop is a participant in the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services' ACCESS model. Ahmed said members 65 and older are actually Whoop's most highly engaged demographic, challenging the assumption that consumer health technology primarily appeals to younger people.

"It's clearly a population that cares a lot about their health. They want to focus on what's going on with their blood pressure, their ECG, or whether they need to send data to their doctors," he said.

Ahmed framed CMS' ACCESS model as a move from consumers simply paying for a wearable toward government reimbursement tied to measurable health outcomes, such as improvements in blood pressure or weight.

"I think as a model of innovation for a government and its citizens, it's pretty interesting because it incentivizes companies to actually create technology or programs that are making people healthier. It should change the cost curve because you're paying if that outcome is delivered, and then to the consumer, you're both hopefully being healthier and not paying for a product that otherwise would have had to," he noted.

Whoop also positions itself as a platform that can wrap around drugs and other healthcare interventions. The manufacturer announced this week a partnership with Novo Nordisk as part of the pharma company's redesign of its direct-to-consumer NovoCare program. Novo Nordisk relaunched its NovoCare direct-to-consumer program. Patients taking a GLP-1 can integrate wearable data from Whoop as part of their program.

Whoop can function as a potential companion for GLP-1 owners, monitoring exercise, sleep, resting heart rate, HRV and other signals while helping users preserve health and fitness during treatment, Ahmed said.

Sources indicate that when asked about the future vision for Whoop, he remarked, "I think in simple terms, it's our responsibility to build technology that either makes you healthier or one day saves your life. You're going to have all of this health data on your body. I think organizing that information in one place, alongside 24/7 wearable data, and alongside a powerful AI that can sit on top of that data and go off on your behalf and take actions and schedule appointments with the doctor, or go speak to your doctor on your behalf, or alert you when something's wrong," he said.

He added, "God forbid this day comes, but you should wake up and be told from Whoop you need to go to the doctor in the next 30 minutes, and it's been scheduled, and you show up, and all of a sudden you find out that you're having a heart attack, or you're having some serious life event. To me, that feels like an inevitable future, and I do predict that a large percentage of humanity in the future will be wearing a continuous health monitor.".

Business as usual for Nvidia as it beats expectations in first earnings call after Huang’s resignation

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, nvidia Corp.
  • The results were so impressive that they slammed the brakes on a weeklong slide, as Nvidia’s stock rose more than 4% in late trading today.
  • It has been revealed that the chipmaker reported third-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $2.68 per share, surpassing Wall Street’s target of $2.48 per share by a comfortable margin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:49 EST / NOVEMBER 17 2026.

According to recent reports, nvidia Corp. delivered earnings and revenue that surpassed Wall Street’s expectations and offered strong guidance for the current quarter in its first earnings call since the shocking resignation of its iconic co-founder and Chief Executive Jensen Huang.

The results were so impressive that they slammed the brakes on a weeklong slide, as Nvidia’s stock rose more than 4% in late trading today.

It has been revealed that the chipmaker reported third-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $2.68 per share, surpassing Wall Street’s target of $2.48 per share by a comfortable margin. Revenue for the period came to $115.84 billion, more than double a year earlier and above the $109.1 billion consensus estimate.

Sources indicate that the vast majority of those sales stemmed from Nvidia’s core data center business, which delivered revenue of $107.6 billion, higher than the Street’s $101.87 billion forecast. For the current quarter, Nvidia remarked it’s expecting its revenue to grow by about 90%, to $130 billion. Though that suggests a slowdown sequentially from the prior quarter, it’s still nicely above Wall Street’s target of $125.1 billion.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress (pictured, with Huang in the background) has become a familiar face to analysts on Nvidia’s conference calls, but today she found herself in a very different position. For the first time, she was fielding questions as the firm’s interim CEO, which means her responsibilities now go well beyond the numbers. She was joined on the call by Nvidia’s Chairman of the Board Harvey Jones, who insisted that the board has no intention of bringing Huang back as CEO.

According to recent reports, nvidia has been under a cloud all week following the abrupt resignation of Huang, which came days after he admitted to having an affair with a businesswoman who’s alleged to be a Chinese spy. In the days that followed that scandal, which included rumors of a second affair with an Nvidia executive and also a potential third fling with yet another company employee, the chipmaker’s stock had been in a downward spiral. But that trend was finally reversed following the company’s strong guidance today.

According to recent reports, one of the central questions investors had going into the call was if Nvidia would scrap its previous forecast for 70% revenue growth in the fiscal year ending January 2028. However, Kress did the opposite and raised the tech giant’s full-year guidance to 75% growth.

In raising the tech giant’s outlook, Kress told analysts on the call that “it’s business as usual at Nvidia,” despite all that has happened. And indeed, throughout much of her commentary, she focused strictly to the numbers that revealed a business still in good health. With regard to the guidance, Kress stressed that this forecast “considers data center readiness, the strength and durability of customer demand and our customers’ access to capital.”.

Sources indicate that “Our leadership has stood up so strongly over the last week to support both what we are doing here at earnings, but also supporting all of our different employees around the world,” Kress noted. “Remember, we have the best technologists on the planet with a world-class, multiyear roadmap. And I think that’s key from a business perspective.”.

Kress said Nvidia expects frontier labs such as OpenAI Group PBC, Anthropic Group PBC and others to account for about 15% of its data center revenue this year, in a sign that they’re increasingly standing up their own data center infrastructure rather than renting from cloud providers.

“As frontier models become more capable, adoption and revenue are scaling rapidly, with Anthropic annualized revenue reaching $181 billion at the end of October,” Kress said.

According to recent reports, another big chunk of Nvidia’s revenue comes from so-called neocloud infrastructure providers. Much of the money those customers spend on its chips stems from a complex web of financing, with much of it being traceable back to Nvidia itself. Kress told analysts that the organization is continuing to help neoclouds and frontier labs to secure the land, power and data center capacity they need to grow, and that it may be willing to share revenue from neoclouds together with the upfront sales of its products, if they meet certain conditions.

Kress said Nvidia currently has more than $32 billion in total commitments to neoclouds through 2032, but insisted that these take effect only if those customers are able to “secure the funding they need to purchase the data center infrastructure products they require, and if the related compute capacity is deployed and made operational.”.

Another closely watched number is Nvidia’s gross margin, which has narrowed in recent quarters as its supply commitments have slowly piled up. Investors will have been pleased to see that Nvidia beat Wall Street’s expectations on that metric, with its nonstandard gross margin ending the quarter at 74.9%, above the forecast of 74%. Its margins still declined compared to the previous quarter, though, blamed on the ramping up of production of its latest generation Rubin graphics processing units.

Industry observers note that the results prove that AI demand remains as strong as ever. But the bigger question for the market now is not how long Nvidia can sustain its growth, rather whether or not it can sustain its current level of profitability, Forrester analyst Naveen Chhabra told SiliconANGLE.

Industry observers note that “The next battle is not against competitors. Nvidia must navigate export controls, sovereign AI initiatives, supply chain expansion and rising capital intensity, all while trying to protect its industry-leading margins,” Chhabra said. “Nvidia continues to defy gravity with triple-digit growth, software-like margins and a strong outlook despite trade restrictions. The next test is whether it can preserve its economic dominance as geopolitics and AI infrastructure costs rise.”.

Despite the after-hours gain, Nvidia’s stock is still down 24% this month, and last Friday it completed its sixth successive weekly decline. That’s the tech giant’s longest losing streak since 2012, and its shares are now trading at their lowest level since July 2025.

It has been revealed that the decline began several weeks before news of Huang’s extramarital escapades became public knowledge. The manufacturer has also faced rising concerns about a possible slowdown in the artificial intelligence industry and a political shift in Washington D.C. as a result of the Republicans’ stunning losses during the midterm elections earlier this month.

Despite Jones’ insistence that Huang will not be returning to the CEO role, the prospect of his doing so cannot be ruled out. In his first public comments since his ousting, Huang said in a post on X that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the tech giant, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”.

According to recent reports, there are plenty of people who would like to see Huang return, including U.S. President Donald Trump and various luminaries from the technology world. Last Thursday, someone created an online petition calling for the reinstatement of Huang, and it has been signed by names including Elon Musk, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan and Epic Games Inc. CEO Tim Sweeney.

According to recent reports, it could be possible that Huang ends up returning to the company in a different capacity than CEO. Susquehanna analyst Chris Rolland told CNBC that the chipmaker could end up taking him back under a upcoming role, such as a consultant or a strategic adviser.

“I think that helps bridge the gap here, he can give technical and strategic advisory services that I think would be incredibly important to the firm,” the analyst said.

Savannah Chrisley has confirmed that her due date is in "10 weeks"—after announcing that she and her husband, Jason Galanis, had tied the knot and were expecting a baby boy.

The 29-year-old real estate agent, who shot to fame alongside her parents, Todd and Julie Chrisley, on their reality TV show, "Chrisley Knows Best," announced on Oct. 27 that she was both pregnant and engaged to Galanis, who is 27 years her senior and served time behind bars alongside her father.

Days later, it was revealed that they are actually married, with People reporting that they remarked "I do" on July 14—just one year after beginning their romance.

Then, it was reported that the couple had snapped up a $2.2 million family home in Nashville.

Now, the TV personality has revealed that she is expected to welcome her son in just "10 weeks" in an Instagram post, in which she joked she was "a little more than half baked" while she and her spouse chewed on chocolate chips.

"Okay so maybe a little more than half baked. Can’t believe we only have 10 weeks until baby boy arrives! Your daddy and I cannot wait to meet you, sweet boy," she captioned the post.

In the carousel of snaps, the couple could be seen embracing as they held up their sonogram photos.

Just two weeks ago, Chrisley declared the gender of her child in a touching social media post, which she captioned, “It's a boy! My sweet miracle boy, you are everything we prayed for and more. The most beautiful reminder that God’s plans are always greater than our own.".

It has been revealed that in the video, the couple could be seen laying on a blanket and embracing each other. It then cut to them cutting a white cake that read "baby" to reveal the blue icing inside.

"The past few days have reminded me just how cruel this world can be. But no amount of hate could ever overshadow the joy of loving you. You are a MIRACLE. My precious baby boy, your daddy and I will spend the rest of our lives protecting you, praying over you, and loving you beyond measure. We may not be able to shield you from every bit of darkness in this world, but we promise to raise you to be a LIGHT in it.You are already our greatest blessing, our answered prayer, and the sweetest chapter of our lives," the mom to be penned in the caption.

She ended the post with the words, "God knew what He was doing when He gave us YOU. We get to be your mommy and daddy.".

Recent findings suggest that during an appearance on "The Golden Ticket," Chrisley admitted that the couple avoided filing their marriage paperwork in the U.S. so that they could keep the news to themselves.

“I’m not public about anything. We ended up getting married in the Cayman Islands in July. So we did everything there, but we haven’t filed [in the U.S.] because then it will be public record, right?" she noted.

Despite having already tied the knot, she revealed that they plan to have another celebration in May.

“The wedding is in May. The wedding was supposed to be in January, [but] I have a real-life wedding crasher,” she remarked as she motioned toward her baby bump.

It was previously revealed that the couple began putting roots down for their family home months before she declared her pregnancy, with the soon-to-be parents picking up a $2.2 million pad in February, as first reported by TMZ.

The 5,207-square-foot property was built in 2023 and comes with five bedrooms and 5.5 bathrooms. It includes two fireplaces, chic wood and marble flooring, walk-in closets, and a chef's kitchen with state-of-the-art appliances.

It also features a patio, balcony, and two-car garage.

The home was listed for $2.9 million in June 2025, meaning the expectant mother got over a half-million dollars off.

After her husband's identity was revealed, Chrisley opened up about their romance on her podcast, "Unlocked," telling her fans that she doesn't pay any mind to their large age gap.

"Yes, there is a huge age gap there, OK? And that’s probably part of the reason why I kept a lot of it quiet, because I know how brutal the public can be. But I genuinely do not care," she insisted.

Industry observers note that "I have always said, ‘I would rather [have] 20 phenomenal, unbelievable years with someone than 50 ‘meh’ years.' Like, the amount of love and respect that we have, we have so many dreams, and we dream together, we work together ... we want to have life experiences with each other. And I think that’s when you know you have the right person, when you don’t feel like you have to escape them at times. We do everything together. ... And it’s just such an amazing, fulfilling feeling to finally find your person. And I’m there. So, yes, the age difference. So what?".

Chrisley also shed some light on his proposal, which came a mere five months into their relationship.

"When he gave me the ring, he was like, ‘Before I open this, I just want you to know that this is just an expression of love to you. This can be whatever you want it to be. This can be an engagement ring, a promise ring, a cocktail ring for all I care. I just want you to know how much I love you,'" she noted. "And there was no pressure ever put on me to, like, ‘You have to accept this as this.'".

Although she acknowledged that the engagement took place fairly early in their relationship, she added, "timing means nothing.".

Chrisley announced the news of her pregnancy on Oct. 27 via an adorable Instagram post.

In a recent development, “I’ve prayed for this life. I’ve cried for this life. And there were moments I truly wondered if this life would ever be mine. And just when I thought my heart couldn’t hold any ›more love, God gave us our sweetest blessing yet ... we’re having a BABY!," Chrisley remarked in the social media post announcing the news, which saw her cradling her baby bump while sitting on her kitchen island and kissing Galanis.

In a recent development, “The past few years have taken me through fires I never imagined I’d have to walk through. Seasons of heartbreak, loss, and moments when I didn’t know if I would ever make it to the other side. I wondered if I would ever find my forever ... if I would ever feel safe enough to truly breathe again. And then God sent me J," she added.

Sources indicate that “My protector. My fiercest fighter. My most loyal person. My lover. My safe place. A man with the patience of Job (and Lord knows he needs it). The one who makes me laugh even on my hardest days. For the first time in a long time, I feel safe. I feel fulfilled. I can finally exhale. I found my forever in you," Chrisley said.

The TV personality then took a moment to praise her partner for how caring he has been during her pregnancy: “J, watching the way you already love and protect our baby before he/she has even entered this world has made me fall in love with you in an entirely fresh way. Not a single doctor’s appointment missed. Constantly caring for me, talking about our baby, and reminding me how beautiful my growing bump is. I thank God every day that this baby gets to call you Daddy.".

“I once prayed just to make it through another day. Now I get to spend forever with the love of my life, carrying a little miracle we already love more than words. From heartbreak to healing. From surviving to living. From praying for my forever to building a family with him. Only God could have written this story. Here’s to forever, J ... and the sweetest little blessing we can’t wait to meet," she added.

Chrisley had kept the identity of her partner under wraps until now, having previously revealed on her podcast, "Unlocked with Savannah Chrisley,"  that she wouldn't share his name "until after I'm married.".

In the latest episode of her podcast, she revealed she and Jason began their romance last July, branding it a "dream relationship.".

Industry observers note that she revealed that Galanis proposed five months into their relationship when they were in the Cayman Islands. "The ring is insane and it’s everything I ever wanted.".

She then revealed that the couple connected after Jason reached out to her to praise her for her efforts to get her parents out of prison.

Todd and Julie Chrisley were found guilty in 2022 of conspiring to defraud Georgia banks out of more than $36 million in personal loans and tax evasion, before being pardoned by President Donald Trump in May 2025.

Savannah Chrisley has frequently spoken out about the toll of her parents' incarceration.

Todd, 57, was sentenced to 12 years (later reduced to 10 years) in the Federal Correctional Institution Pensacola in Florida. Julie, 53, was sentenced to seven years in the Federal Medical Center in Lexington, KY.

Following her parents' incarceration, Savannah took on the care of her brother, Grayson, 19, and her niece, Chloe, 13, while also assuming responsibility for the care and maintenance of her parents' opulent dwelling.

At the same time, the burgeoning real estate agent was tirelessly campaigning for Todd and Julie's release, issuing public pleas for government support, while alleging that her parents were being subjected to "beyond inhumane" conditions behind bars.

Industry observers note that on May 27, her prayers were answered when Trump revealed to her in a personal phone call that he planned to pardon her parents. Just a few days later, they were released from prison.

At the time, Savannah revealed she was ready to return the hefty upkeep of their home to Todd and Julie.

#29997. Latest Update: Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1364 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1364 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that energy drinks and stimulant supplements are raising new concerns about heart health after researchers discovered a striking pattern in reports of serious cardiovascular emergencies.
  • Recent findings suggest that the findings were particularly concerning among younger adults.
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers emphasized that the findings do not establish that energy drinks or stimulant supplements caused these medical emergencies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that energy drinks and stimulant supplements are raising new concerns about heart health after researchers discovered a striking pattern in reports of serious cardiovascular emergencies. Products containing caffeine and other stimulants appeared far more frequently in reports of cardiac arrest, heart attacks, and other heart problems than products without these ingredients.

Recent findings suggest that the findings were particularly concerning among younger adults. People ages 18 to 34 accounted for a substantial share of the reported heart problems involving caffeinated products, according to independent, preliminary research presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026.

Recent findings suggest that researchers emphasized that the findings do not establish that energy drinks or stimulant supplements caused these medical emergencies. However, the unusually high frequency of certain cardiovascular events in FDA safety reports suggests that these widely available products deserve closer examination.

Growing Concerns About Energy Drinks and Heart Health.

The energy drink industry has expanded rapidly, with sales more than doubling over the past decade and exceeding $20 billion in 2024. Despite their popularity, scientists still have limited information about the cardiovascular effects of energy drinks and supplements containing stimulants.

Existing evidence suggests that consuming large amounts of caffeine can harm the cardiovascular system. Medical professionals have also documented cases of arrhythmias (irregular heart rhythms) and sudden cardiac death following the consumption of these products. Some of these incidents involved young adults who had no previously identified risk factors for heart disease.

A 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease indicates that most adults can generally consume up to 400 mg of caffeine daily without significant safety concerns (the equivalent of up to 5, 8-ounce cups of regular black caffeinated coffee).

Sources indicate that however, caffeine concentrations can differ dramatically between products. Certain energy drinks provide up to three times as much caffeine per fluid ounce as brewed coffee, while some pre-workout supplements contain more than 12 times the concentration found in coffee.

Another concern involves how these products are regulated. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) classifies energy drinks and stimulant supplements as foods or dietary supplements rather than medications. As a result, they are not subject to the same safety testing requirements that medications must meet before entering the market.

According to recent reports, "These products are marketed as everyday pick-me-ups and sold next to soda and bottled water, so most people assume they carry no real risk," said study author Sai Samayamanthula, a fourth-year medical student at the University of Virginia School of Medicine in Charlottesville, Virginia. "For many healthy people, if these products are consumed occasionally, the risk is probably small. However, individuals who consume energy drinks or other stimulant-containing supplements regularly can swiftly exceed the recommended daily limit for caffeine, so it's important for people to know that there may be a risk of cardiovascular harm with these products.".

FDA Reports Reveal Striking Differences in Cardiac Events.

According to recent reports, to investigate possible cardiovascular safety concerns, researchers examined a federal database containing reports of suspected adverse reactions to foods and dietary supplements. They compared products containing caffeine and other stimulants with products that did not contain these ingredients.

The comparison group included commonly consumed products such as soft drinks, smoothies, vitamins, protein bars, and meal replacement shakes. Researchers examined reports involving people ages 13 and older submitted between 2017 and 2025.

Several differences stood out in the analysis:.

These differences describe how frequently certain medical problems appeared within the FDA reports. They do not mean that people consuming energy drinks face an 11 times greater actual risk of cardiac arrest or a 4.5 times greater risk of having a heart attack.

According to recent reports, "Our findings support the case for more systematic safety monitoring of caffeine- and stimulant-containing products. In addition, healthcare professionals should remember to ask their younger patients who have palpitations, chest pain, or fainting spells if they recently or regularly consume these products," Samayamanthula stated.

Why Young Adults May Be Particularly Vulnerable.

According to recent reports, one of the most notable findings was the large proportion of cardiovascular reports involving younger adults. Researchers have not yet determined why the connection between stimulant products and reported heart problems appeared so frequently in this age group.

Several explanations are possible. Younger consumers may use energy drinks and stimulant supplements more often, increasing the likelihood that these products appear in reports of medical emergencies.

How the products are consumed could also influence the pattern. Potential contributing factors include the circumstances surrounding their use (for example, consuming them before intense exercise or mixing them with alcohol or drugs). Some individuals may also have previously undiagnosed heart conditions that could make them more susceptible to cardiovascular complications.

These possibilities remain uncertain, and additional research will be needed to determine which factors, if any, help explain the unusually high reporting frequency among younger adults.

Do Energy Drinks Actually Cause Heart Attacks?

Although the results raise key questions about products containing concentrated caffeine and other stimulants, experts caution against interpreting the findings as proof of a direct cause.

"This study raises concerns that products with very high amounts of caffeine may be harmful to the cardiovascular system," remarked Gregory M. Marcus, M.D., M.A.S., FAHA, chair of the 2026 American Heart Association scientific statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease. "Although there are biological reasons why that connection could be possible, the study does not prove that caffeine products cause these events, because other factors may have influenced the results found in this analysis. More research is needed to understand whether these stimulant products are truly responsible for the reported heart-related events.".

Marcus did not participate in the research. He is a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine and serves as associate chief of the Cardiology for Research program at the University of California, San Francisco Health.

Recent findings suggest that because the analysis relied on reports submitted voluntarily to the FDA, it cannot establish whether the products themselves were responsible for the cardiovascular events. Other health conditions, behaviors, or circumstances may have played a role.

How Researchers Analyzed the FDA Safety Reports.

The research team reviewed 28,345 reports of possible adverse events submitted to an FDA safety database from 2017 through 2025.

Of these, 854 reports involved energy drinks or dietary supplements containing caffeine or other stimulants. The remaining 27,491 reports concerned products without caffeine or stimulant ingredients and served as the comparison group.

According to recent reports, researchers classified products according to the ingredients they contained. The stimulant category included caffeine, methylxanthines (theobromine, guarana, yerba mate, green tea/coffee extracts) and sympathomimetics (synephrine, yohimbine, ephedra, DMAA, higenamine).

Rather than evaluating individual brands, the researchers grouped products by their ingredients. Consequently, the findings apply to broad categories of caffeinated and stimulant products and do not identify any particular brand as more dangerous than another.

Sources indicate that the researchers also highlighted crucial limitations in the available data. Reports were voluntarily submitted by members of the public, consumers, healthcare professionals, and manufacturers, meaning that the database does not provide a complete record of everyone who experienced a possible adverse reaction.

It has been revealed that just as importantly, the researchers could not determine how many people consumed these products without developing cardiovascular problems. They also could not establish how many people experienced heart problems but never submitted a report.

Without those figures, the analysis cannot calculate the actual likelihood of a heart attack, cardiac arrest, or another cardiovascular event among consumers of energy drinks and stimulant supplements.

According to recent reports, nevertheless, the findings reveal a potentially important safety signal. Researchers say more systematic monitoring and further studies are needed to determine whether these products contribute directly to serious heart problems, particularly among younger adults who frequently consume them.

Homebuilder Confidence Hits New 14-Year Low as High Mortgage Rates and Inflation Take a Toll
