Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1392 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A common sugar found in many foods and sweetened drinks may play an unexpected role in helping aggressive ovarian cancer spread.
  • The findings, published in Nature Aging, reveal a previously unknown way that cancer cells can continue influencing a tumor even after treatment has stopped them from multiplying.
  • It has been revealed that "Some cancer cells that survive chemotherapy aren't dividing anymore, but they're still biologically active," remarked Aidan Cole, Ph.D., a postdoctoral fellow in the lab of Katherine Aird, Ph.D., at The Wistar Institute and first author on the study.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A common sugar found in many foods and sweetened drinks may play an unexpected role in helping aggressive ovarian cancer spread. Researchers at The Wistar Institute have discovered that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy can release fructose, which acts as a signal that encourages nearby tumor cells to break free and spread.

The findings, published in Nature Aging, reveal a previously unknown way that cancer cells can continue influencing a tumor even after treatment has stopped them from multiplying. The discovery also raises key questions about whether dietary sugar and commonly prescribed cholesterol medications could affect how cancer progresses.

It has been revealed that "Some cancer cells that survive chemotherapy aren't dividing anymore, but they're still biologically active," remarked Aidan Cole, Ph.D., a postdoctoral fellow in the lab of Katherine Aird, Ph.D., at The Wistar Institute and first author on the study. "Instead, they continue to release molecules that send signals to nearby cells. Our study is among the first to show that a nutrient -- in this case, fructose -- can act as one of those signals.".

Why Ovarian Cancer Often Returns After Chemotherapy.

It has been revealed that most patients with ovarian cancer receive platinum-based chemotherapy, a treatment that uses drugs containing platinum to damage the DNA of cancer cells and prevent them from reproducing. Although many patients initially respond well, the cancer eventually returns in most cases. It also frequently spreads throughout the abdominal cavity, the space inside the abdomen that contains organs such as the stomach, intestines, and liver.

This spread, known as metastasis, is responsible for approximately 90% of ovarian cancer deaths. Understanding what allows cancer cells to escape from their original location and establish new tumors is therefore a major priority for researchers.

Sources indicate that previous studies have suggested that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy may contribute to recurrence even when they are no longer actively dividing. These surviving cells can continue producing and releasing a mixture of substances that influence the behavior of surrounding cells.

To investigate this process, Cole and his colleagues developed an experiment that separated the surviving cancer cells from the molecules they released. They discovered that these released substances, even without the surviving cells themselves, were enough to significantly increase cancer spread in a preclinical model.

"As far as we know, this is the first time anyone has shown, in a preclinical model rather than just a dish, that it's the molecules these cells release -- not the cells themselves -- that drive the cancer's spread," noted Cole.

A Common Sugar Emerges as a Surprising Cancer Signal.

The next challenge was identifying which substances were responsible for encouraging cancer cells to spread. The researchers discovered an unexpected culprit: fructose.

Fructose is a naturally occurring sugar found in fruit, honey, and other foods. It is also a component of table sugar and high fructose corn syrup, a sweetener frequently used in soft drinks and processed foods.

It has been revealed that the study revealed that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy could produce fructose and release it into their surroundings. Rather than simply serving as an energy source, the sugar acted as a chemical messenger that encouraged neighboring cancer cells to become more capable of spreading.

In a recent development, the researchers also uncovered another concerning possibility. In their preclinical experiments, consuming high amounts of fructose comparable to those found in sugary drinks could promote signals associated with cancer spread even without chemotherapy treatment.

This observation suggests that diet might influence cancer progression through a mechanism scientists had not previously recognized. Fructose consumption is particularly relevant in the United States, where high fructose corn syrup can account for approximately 8% to 20% of daily calorie intake in some individuals.

Industry observers note that unlike many factors that influence cancer risk and progression, dietary fructose intake can be changed. That raises the possibility that nutritional strategies might eventually become part of efforts to limit cancer spread.

However, researchers have not yet tested whether reducing fructose consumption improves outcomes in patients with ovarian cancer. The findings do not establish that eating sugar causes cancer to spread in humans, and additional research is needed before specific dietary recommendations can be made based on this mechanism.

How Fructose Helps Cancer Cells Break Free.

To understand how fructose encourages cancer spread, the researchers examined what happens inside cancer cells exposed to the sugar.

They used several advanced methods to investigate the biological changes involved, including a CRISPR screen. This technique allows scientists to systematically examine genes and identify which ones influence a particular cellular process.

The experiments revealed that fructose suppresses cholesterol production in neighboring cancer cells.

It has been revealed that although cholesterol is often discussed in connection with heart disease, it also serves essential functions throughout the body. It is an important component of cell membranes, the thin outer layers that surround cells and help regulate how they interact with their environment.

Industry observers note that in this case, cholesterol helps maintain the connections that hold neighboring cells together. These connections act somewhat like biological glue, making it harder for cancer cells to separate from one another.

When fructose reduces cholesterol production, those connections weaken. As a result, cancer cells can detach more easily, potentially allowing them to escape and spread to other locations.

This discovery provides a possible explanation for how a common nutrient can influence one of the most dangerous aspects of cancer.

A Surprising Connection Between Statins and Cancer Spread.

The cholesterol finding also led researchers to investigate an unexpected question involving statins, medications widely prescribed to lower cholesterol.

In a recent development, approximately 39 million people in the United States take statins. These drugs work by reducing the body's production of cholesterol and are commonly used to lower the risk of heart attacks and strokes.

Because fructose appeared to promote cancer spread by suppressing cholesterol production, the research team wanted to know whether statins might produce similar effects.

Their experiments showed that statins alone could weaken the connections between cancer cells, making it easier for them to separate and escape.

The finding raises questions about whether cholesterol-lowering medications could influence the effectiveness of chemotherapy in certain situations. Researchers are now investigating that possibility, but they emphasize that the results have not been demonstrated in patients and are not a reason for anyone to discontinue prescribed statins.

"We haven't tested this effect in patients yet, but it raises questions about combining cholesterol-lowering drugs with chemotherapy, especially since ovarian cancer is most common in postmenopausal women who are often already on statins," mentioned Katherine Aird, Ph.D., professor and co-leader of the Molecular and Cellular Oncogenesis Program in the Ellen and Ronald Caplan Cancer Center at The Wistar Institute, and senior author of the study.

Could Fructose Also Help Other Cancers Spread?

Although the research focused on ovarian cancer, the scientists suspect that the same biological process could occur in other forms of the disease.

Cancers affecting organs within the abdomen and torso can also spread to nearby tissues and organs. If fructose influences the connections between cancer cells in a similar way, the discovery could have implications beyond ovarian cancer.

According to recent reports, "We think other cancers that spread within the torso -- pancreatic, colon, liver -- could behave similarly. We can't call it universal yet, but we think the effects are not just limited to ovarian cancer," said Aird.

Aird and Cole have already begun designing additional experiments to determine whether their findings can be reproduced in pancreatic, colon, liver, and other cancers.

The research opens a fresh avenue for understanding how cancer spreads, particularly after chemotherapy. It also suggests that the relationship between nutrients, cholesterol production, and cancer cell behavior may be more complicated than previously understood.

While the potential implications for diet and medication remain uncertain, identifying fructose as a signal that helps cancer cells break free could eventually point researchers toward newly introduced strategies for preventing metastasis and improving cancer treatment.

Breaking: U.S. Chamber Backs Capital Gains Tax Exclusion Bill Aimed To Reduce Taxes on Profits From Home Sales

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chamber of Commerce has confirmed support for reducing taxes on the profits homeowners make on the sale of their home, saying it could stimulate more home sales.
  • It has been revealed that raising the capital gains tax exclusion—something hundreds of members of Congress and a number of real estate groups have pushed for this year—is one key lever that Washington, DC hasn't yet pulled.
  • In a recent development, "Capital gains taxes tend to distort housing choices by discouraging individuals from selling their homes because of changing family or health circumstances," the group noted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. Chamber of Commerce has confirmed support for reducing taxes on the profits homeowners make on the sale of their home, saying it could stimulate more home sales.

It has been revealed that raising the capital gains tax exclusion—something hundreds of members of Congress and a number of real estate groups have pushed for this year—is one key lever that Washington, DC hasn't yet pulled. It could have major implications for the housing market, the Chamber mentioned.

In a recent development, "Capital gains taxes tend to distort housing choices by discouraging individuals from selling their homes because of changing family or health circumstances," the group noted. "And the taxation of capital gains in excess of exemption caps creates inequities between homeowners with different job circumstances and those living in different parts of the country.".

It has been revealed that the most visible effort in Congress comes from the More Homes on the Market Act, sponsored by Rep. Jimmy Panetta (R-CA), which would double the current exclusion. Realtor.com® has reached out to his office for comment.

According to recent reports, both the Senate and the House have versions of the bill, which are almost identical. The Chamber stated that bill offers a "reasonable, cost-effective solution" to spur more home sales.

It has been revealed that the two versions have picked up 186 sponsors and cosponsors in Congress, including large numbers of Democrats and Republicans. Earlier this year, Panetta acknowledged the push faces resistance. A congressional analysis from last year estimated such a change could deprive the government of $46.4 billion in tax revenue. Even a more targeted approach, like raising the exclusion only for people over 55, could still cost $4.9 billion.

The National Association of Realtors® also champions the bill to change the tax scheme, because it could allow more people to sell their homes without incurring a punishing tax bill. Kevin Brown, president of NAR, lobbied for the law as he spoke to a panel in Congress in June.

Congress set the current capital gains scheme in 1997. Sellers can exclude up to $250,000 in profit if single, or $500,000 if married and filing jointly, when they sell a primary home, with few strings attached.

But the law didn't include adjustments for inflation. As home prices have appreciated in the years since, homeowners see a mounting impact. The longer the value of their home appreciates, the larger the cut the federal government can take as a capital gains tax when they do sell.

Recent findings suggest that oftentimes, these might be older Americans whose lifestyle might support downsizing. But they're "locked in" to their homes thanks to high mortgage rates.

That causes large tax bills, especially for those who have stayed in their homes the longest. Or, those who live in areas where home prices have grown the fastest. NAR has estimated that nearly 13 million homeowners would face a tax penalty if they sold their homes today. Brown argued that raising the exclusion limits would help free up housing inventory at a time when the country is facing a major supply crunch.

"Capital gains indexing has huge bipartisan support," Colin Allen, executive director of the American Property Owners Alliance told Realtor.com. He brought up the possibility that it might appear in the next Congress in the form of a reintroduced bill or as a part of a reconciliation package.

"It would certainly unlock a number of homes immediately and free up their owners to do something else once they retire, and help families looking to make that next move," Allen noted.

#29969. Without this protein, damaged muscle fills with fat and scar tissue

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1342 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Without this protein, damaged muscle fills with fat and scar tissue

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1342 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When muscles are injured, the body normally activates specialized stem cells that help rebuild damaged tissue.
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers at the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania have identified an unexpected role for a protein called TRF2, which was previously known primarily for protecting chromosomes.
  • The discovery, published in Science Advances, could provide latest directions for muscular dystrophy treatments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When muscles are injured, the body normally activates specialized stem cells that help rebuild damaged tissue. But scientists have discovered that without one critical protein, this repair system can break down, leaving injured muscles filled with fat and scar tissue instead of healthy muscle.

Recent findings suggest that researchers at the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania have identified an unexpected role for a protein called TRF2, which was previously known primarily for protecting chromosomes. Their findings suggest that TRF2 is also essential for maintaining the identity of muscle stem cells, allowing them to continue repairing and regenerating muscle throughout life.

The discovery, published in Science Advances, could provide latest directions for muscular dystrophy treatments. It may also help scientists understand important differences between muscle regeneration and cancer, including why skeletal muscle can repair itself so effectively while cancers originating in muscle are relatively uncommon.

"For years, TRF2 has been viewed as a protein whose primary job is protecting the ends of chromosomes from damage or corruption," noted senior author Foteini Mourkioti, PhD, an associate professor of Orthopedic Surgery at Penn Medicine. "But rather than simply protecting DNA, TRF2 seems to be key to regenerating muscle throughout life.".

A Hidden Protein With an Unexpected Role in Muscle Repair.

For years, scientists have studied TRF2 because of its role in safeguarding telomeres, the protective structures found at the ends of chromosomes. Chromosomes carry our genetic information, and telomeres help keep their ends from deteriorating or being mistaken for damaged DNA.

Sources indicate that the new research highlights that TRF2 has another important responsibility. It helps muscle stem cells retain the genetic instructions that make them muscle stem cells in the first place. Maintaining that identity is essential because these specialized cells serve as the body's reserve supply for repairing injured muscle.

Under normal conditions, muscle stem cells spend much of their time inactive. When an injury occurs, they become active, multiply, and help replace damaged muscle tissue. Some then return to a resting state, preserving a population of stem cells that can respond to future injuries.

Through laboratory experiments, the researchers found that TRF2 levels change as muscle stem cells move between these different stages. The protein's activity rises and falls as the cells transition from dormancy to repair and then replenish themselves, suggesting that TRF2 helps regulate the entire regeneration process.

Without TRF2, Damaged Muscles Accumulate Fat and Scar Tissue.

To understand how notable TRF2 is, the scientists removed the protein from muscle stem cells in laboratory mice. At first, the animals' muscles appeared normal, suggesting that the loss of TRF2 did not immediately damage existing muscle tissue.

Sources indicate that over time, however, a serious problem emerged. The population of functional muscle stem cells began to decline, leaving the animals increasingly unable to repair damaged muscle.

Sources indicate that the researchers initially expected the cells to die, since losing TRF2 can produce that outcome in other tissues. Instead, they discovered something more surprising: the cells remained alive but lost the molecular identity that allowed them to function as muscle stem cells.

In effect, the cells no longer maintained the biological program needed to perform their specialized repair duties.

Sources indicate that the consequences became clear when the muscles were injured. Rather than rebuilding healthy muscle, the damaged tissue accumulated fat and scar tissue, a form of tissue replacement that cannot restore normal muscle function.

"This completely changes how we think about TRF2's role in these cells," stated Mourkioti. "The loss of identity has severe implications for whether recovery from injury is even possible.".

A Potential Breakthrough for Muscular Dystrophy Research.

The team also investigated whether TRF2 plays a role in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a serious inherited disorder that causes progressive muscle weakness and degeneration. The disease interferes with the body's ability to maintain healthy muscles, making effective repair especially important.

Using a mouse model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, the researchers removed TRF2 from muscle stem cells and observed a dramatic worsening of the disease.

Recent findings suggest that muscle degeneration progressed much faster, and the affected mice had shorter survival times. These findings indicate that TRF2 plays an notable role in preserving the regenerative capacity of muscles already struggling with a serious genetic disease.

The results do not yet establish a fresh treatment for muscular dystrophy. However, they identify a biological mechanism that researchers may eventually be able to target to help preserve muscle stem cell function and improve tissue repair.

How TRF2 Protects the Identity of Muscle Stem Cells.

Further experiments revealed how TRF2 performs this unexpected function.

Industry observers note that although the protein is best known for working at the ends of chromosomes, the researchers found that it also attaches to regulatory regions throughout the genome. These regions help control which genes are active or inactive, determining how cells behave and what specialized functions they perform.

Sources indicate that for muscle stem cells, this regulation is particularly vital. Their ability to repair muscle depends on maintaining a specific pattern of gene activity that preserves their identity and regenerative potential.

In a recent development, the scientists discovered that many of the DNA regions associated with TRF2 contain unusual structures known as G-quadruplexes. These structures form when sections of DNA rich in the building block guanine fold into distinctive arrangements involving four interacting strands or segments.

According to recent reports, G-quadruplexes have attracted considerable scientific interest because they can influence how genes function. They are also being investigated as possible targets for cancer treatments.

The Penn researchers found that TRF2 interacts with these specialized DNA structures to help maintain the genetic program that keeps muscle stem cells functioning properly.

"We found that TRF2 works through these secondary DNA structures to preserve the identity of muscle stem cells and keep them capable of repairing damaged muscle," Mourkioti noted. "That was completely unexpected.".

What Muscle Regeneration Could Reveal About Cancer.

Beyond muscular dystrophy, the discovery may help researchers investigate a longstanding mystery about muscle biology.

Skeletal muscle, the type of muscle that allows the body to move, has an impressive ability to regenerate after injury. Yet cancers that originate in skeletal muscle are relatively rare, even though other tissues with substantial regenerative activity can be more vulnerable to cancer.

This raises an important question: how can muscle maintain such a powerful repair system without frequently developing cancer?

The researchers believe that TRF2's unusual role in muscle stem cells could offer clues. By examining how the protein regulates gene activity in muscle compared with other tissues, scientists may gain a better understanding of the mechanisms that support regeneration while limiting the risk of uncontrolled cell growth.

That distinction matters because cancer develops when cells acquire changes that allow them to grow and divide without the normal biological restraints. Finding ways to strengthen muscle repair without encouraging abnormal growth would be an vital goal for future therapies.

Recent findings suggest that mourkioti and her colleagues are now investigating whether the way muscle stem cells use TRF2 could lead to new treatment strategies for muscular dystrophy. They also hope to determine what this mechanism can reveal about cancer biology in tissues that are more susceptible to the disease.

Although additional research is needed to determine whether these findings can be translated into treatments for people, the discovery reveals an notable part of the body's muscle repair system. It also demonstrates that a protein long associated with protecting DNA has a much broader role in keeping muscles capable of healing.

The research was supported by grants from the National Institutes of Health/ National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (R01 DK123356, R01s CA174904, GM101149, and FDN-143330).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:58 EST / NOVEMBER 17 2026.

Recent findings suggest that brain-computer interface manufacturer Science Corp. today revealed it has raised $400 million in a late-stage round of funding that brings its valuation to $3.5 billion.

In a recent development, the Series D round, declared in a blog post today, was led by high-profile venture capital firm Khosla Ventures. It was joined by the Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare, 885 Capital, Y Combinator and PLC Neurotech. The Ackman Oxman Institute’s participation is notable, as it appears to be one of brain research center’s first ventures after being established by the hedge fund billionaire Bill Ackman and his wife Neri Oxman earlier this year.

In a recent development, the money from today’s round will give Science the capital it needs to bring its flagship product PRIMA to the U.S. healthcare market, having already established traction in Europe. PRIMA is a specialized chip that’s implanted into the eyes of patients suffering from age-related macular degeneration or AMD, which is one of the most common causes of vision loss among older adults. It’s paired with a special pair of glasses that help restore partial vision to AMD sufferers, and it has already been approved by some European countries.

Sources indicate that for instance, PRIMA has already been implanted in the eyes of several patients in Germany, and the manufacturer has dozens of additional surgical procedures scheduled to help more patients restore their vision. In addition, the device is expected to be made available in Italy, France and the U.K. in the coming months. Science wants to offer PRIMA to patients who are willing to pay for it out of pocket at a special unit at Moorfields Private Eye Hospital in London, but it has not disclosed how much people would have to pay.

In a recent development, as for the U.S., PRIMA is currently being vetted for its suitability by the Food and Drug Administration. Science founder and Chief Executive Max Hodak, who previously served as the CEO of Elon Musk’s Neuralink Inc., told Bloomberg in an interview today that he’s hoping it will be made available to U.S. patients early next year.

Industry observers note that that’s because PRIMA is being pushed through the FDA’s Humanitarian Device Exemption pathway, which allows for the rapid approval of experimental medical technologies that can treat rare conditions. Though AMD is not uncommon, the tech giant has argued that it’s rare to see the condition affect people in both eyes.

In the future, the organization also plans to make PRIMA available as a treatment for Stargardt’s disease and retinitis pigmentosa, which also cause blindness.

Sources indicate that the PRIMA device consists of 378 pixels that are each equipped with a tiny electrode. When infrared light hits a pixel, it activates the attached electrode, which in turn simulates cells in the patient’s retina. The electrodes thereby substitute for retinal tissue lost to disease.

The infrared light that activates the implant’s pixels comes from a pair of glasses worn by the patient. According to Science, the glasses generate infrared signals based on footage from a forward-facing camera. The camera, which records the user’s surroundings, includes a lens that filters interference such as strong sunlight.

While Science is focused on PRIMA for now, its long-term vision is not limited to restoring people’s sight. It’s also developing the Biohybrid implant, which connects directly to the brain.

It’s built from cultured neurons that are combined with silicon chips and integrated with the brain’s circuits. The tech giant says it has already identified the first disease it intends to treat with Biohybrid but has not disclosed what that condition is.

For now, it’s focused on testing Biohybrid. So far, it has conducted tests only on animals, but it hopes to launch its first human clinical trials within the next 16 months. To do this, it has recruited the respected Yale neurosurgery professor Murat Günel, who has previously remarked that the device holds promise for treating Parkinson’s disease and other brain illnesses and injuries.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A sprawling California ranch where Alex Trebek helped run a winery is heading to auction, giving buyers a chance to purchase nearly 578 acres of the Central Coast once owned by the longtime “Jeopardy!” host.

Known as Creston Manor, the property in San Luis Obispo County near Paso Robles is listed for $6.45 million.

In a press release shared with Realtor.com®, Concierge Auctions revealed bidding is scheduled to open on Dec. 4 and conclude live on Dec. 16 at The Dominick in Newly introduced York City, where the ranch will be offered as part of the organization’s year-end sale.

Lindsey Harn of Christie’s International Real Estate and Mike Goldfarb of Coldwell Banker Residential Brokerage Company are working with the auction house on the sale.

Creston Manor is the second former Trebek property in the area to come up for auction through the firm this year.

It has been revealed that earlier in 2026, Concierge Auctions sold Windfall Farms, a nearly 724-acre property in nearby Paso Robles, for $16.9 million. The auction house stated it marketed that property for 39 days before the sale.

Creston Manor was established in 1900, decades before Trebek became a partner in Creston Manor Vineyards and Winery in 1987.

According to the auction house, the game show host used the property primarily for ranching and wine production.

In a recent development, one vintage detail from the auction announcement ties the ranch to Washington, DC. Concierge Auctions says wine from the estate was served at President George H.W. Bush’s inauguration.

The vineyard and winery are still operational, according to the sale announcement.

The estate also retains parts of its ranching history, including a preserved blacksmith shop and the original Highway 58 bridge.

Those structures sit on the same property as the barns, stables, and livestock facilities that support its current agricultural use.

The ranch covers approximately 577.65 acres, with rolling pastureland and mountain views. Livestock pens are set up to accommodate cattle, horses, sheep, and pigs, and the stables provide dedicated space for horses.

The existing agricultural facilities are a central part of the offering, particularly for buyers who want to continue ranching or producing wine on the property.

Beyond the agricultural buildings, the property has five residences and a separate private suite. Together, the living quarters span approximately 7,550 square feet and contain 14 bedrooms and 14 full bathrooms.

According to Concierge Auctions, the estate can accommodate more than 30 guests.

It has been revealed that that layout gives a buyer several places to house visitors across the ranch. The separate suite adds another option for guests who want more privacy, while the acreage leaves room for substantial pasture alongside the vineyard and residential buildings.

Harn pointed to the combination of housing, winemaking facilities, and equestrian infrastructure as a distinguishing feature of the property.

The ranch is in Creston, a community in northern San Luis Obispo County with agricultural ties of its own. Goldfarb highlighted the estate’s seclusion and its proximity to Paso Robles, where the surrounding wine region is home to more than 200 wineries.

Paso Robles also has a downtown dining scene and the Tin City tasting district. Nearby Santa Margarita Lake offers kayaking, fishing, and hiking.

Concierge Auctions is handling the sale through its division focused on wineries, vineyards, and other wine country real estate.

Creston Manor brings those uses together on a single property, with the working winery and vineyard sharing the acreage with livestock facilities and multiple homes.

Chad Roffers, the auction house’s CEO and co-founder, said the firm hopes to draw international bidders to Creston Manor, just as it did when it brought Windfall Farms to auction earlier this year.

The auction house also claims a closing will trigger a contribution toward building homes for families in need through its Key for Key program, a partnership with Giveback Homes.

Abandoned Property for Sale: How To Buy an Abandoned Home

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (998 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Buying an abandoned property can be a bargain for homebuyers—if you can actually find such a property.
  • Sources indicate that properties that are unclaimed by their owners are potential low-cost purchases that might be attractive to prospective homebuyers.
  • Still, "abandoned house for sale" isn't a sign you're likely to see on the roadside.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buying an abandoned property can be a bargain for homebuyers—if you can actually find such a property.

Sources indicate that properties that are unclaimed by their owners are potential low-cost purchases that might be attractive to prospective homebuyers. They certainly have become all the rage on TikTok, with influencers snatching up properties left and right and sharing their renovation journeys.

Still, "abandoned house for sale" isn't a sign you're likely to see on the roadside. (There might actually be laws against that!).

According to recent reports, an abandoned property is usually a property whose original owner is no longer in possession of the home. Due to the owner's financial difficulties, the house is typically run-down and in desperate need of repair. If the law in your area allows you to claim this type of home and you're handy, it might be worth investigating.

However, some abandoned homes for sale can turn out to be in good condition, with the owner hoping to unload the property before foreclosure. This could provide the right buyer with an opportunity to purchase the abandoned property or unclaimed home at a discount—and possibly a significant return on investment if you later flip it.

Purchasing an abandoned or unclaimed property involves following the same procedures as buying any other piece of real estate. Before setting out on your journey to find an abandoned home, review your financial situation.

Sources indicate that remember, there will be additional expenses over and above the original sale price of the property. A pre-qualification from your bank or lender will help you estimate what mortgage amount you qualify for. Many banks also require pre-approval letters, so you can make quick decisions on the property you wish to purchase.

Most abandoned homes for sale are on their way to foreclosure, but the bank has not yet initiated the process. Various lists of abandoned properties or unclaimed properties are available, or you can search for abandoned foreclosures or pre-foreclosures online.

Check for listings of homes for sale with certain phrases that might indicate an abandoned property, such as "immediate possession," "must sell," "below market value," or "under appraisal." Don't forget to add "near me.".

Real estate agents will usually have valuable knowledge of abandoned properties in the area and the law relating to claiming them, and can provide you with a selection of homes about to be foreclosed on by the bank.

Some properties might look abandoned but are not listed for sale. You might also check into the laws regarding unclaimed property and whether there is a statute of limitations on its return.

If you find an interesting unclaimed property like this, visit your county clerk’s office. It will have information about the homeowners, the home's current appraised value, liens, or tax problems.

Industry observers note that you could then try tracking down the owners and asking them to sell their property. If the property has had liens or tax problems, the owners might be more willing to sell.

According to recent reports, abandoned homes will almost always have complications. Due to months (or years) of neglect, a lack of maintenance, and overall aging, vacant homes are far from pristine. They are often sold as is, which means what you see is what you get.

One major risk? Abandoned homes usually have had their utilities turned off. With no way to check the water, electricity, gas, heating and cooling systems, or appliances, even a professional home inspector will be unable to thoroughly evaluate the house. There could be wiring problems, water leaks, or gas leaks—any of which would be extremely costly to repair.

It might be possible to have utilities turned on temporarily, but that requires paying a deposit and putting the utilities in your name. Even if utilities are turned on, you'll likely have to accept some elements of the abandoned home as is. But remember, forgoing major system inspections is a huge gamble.

A second major risk factor is the deferred maintenance involved with the purchase of a property that's been left to the elements. If previous owners abandoned the home or lost it to foreclosure, they probably didn't pay attention to routine maintenance tasks. Costly repairs will crop up sooner than expected, and you'll have to budget for future repairs.

In a recent development, and to top it off, obtaining home insurance on an abandoned home is difficult. Most insurance agencies won't insure a vacated house without an inspection from one of their agents. And that agent might require you to make costly repairs before issuing a policy.

If the insurer concerns a policy, premiums for an unoccupied structure will likely be significantly higher. Because no one has watched over the home, it's more likely to have suffered vandalism or fire damage. Vacant homes often have broken pipes or leaking roofs with resulting water damage, stolen copper wiring, mold, pest issues, and damaged appliances.

Assuming you have found a potential abandoned property for sale and been pre-approved, you will want to factor in costs that will be needed to get the home into solid condition. Get a thorough maintenance inspection performed on the property, and note what needs to be fixed and how much it will cost.

Claiming a property like this also involves adding in the cost of the appraisal fee, pest and lead inspection fees, title insurance, closing costs, and other legal fees.

According to recent reports, crunch the numbers before you consider a bid. A real estate agent can also accompany you to the abandoned property for sale and point out the extra expenses you will incur after the purchase of this property. The agent can also help you figure out how high your bid should be. Look for the right opportunities, and you might find a home that is just right for your budget.

Angela Colley writes about real estate and all things renting and moving for Realtor.com. Her work has appeared in outlets including TheStreet, MSN, and Yahoo.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The elegant Malibu estate that Google co-founder Sergey Brin purchased with his ex-wife, Nicole Shanahan, has hit the selling block for $33.5 million—months after it was listed as a rental.

Sources indicate that brin, 53, and Shanahan—who went on to join Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s short-lived presidential campaign—bought the "dreamy" Point Dume dwelling for $13.5 million in September 2020, just over a year before it was revealed that they had split after three years of marriage.

It has been revealed that the details of their divorce settlement, which was finalized in 2023, were never fully revealed. However, reports suggest that Shanahan walked away with around $1 billion in assets, including shares in Alphabet, Google's parent company.

It has never been revealed how the former couple split their shared properties. Brin purchased another Malibu residence for $35 million just a few months after their separation, a move that many saw as a sign that Shanahan, 41, had kept their former marital home.

In a recent development, property records viewed by Realtor.com® show that the five-bedroom, 7.5-bathroom dwelling is currently registered to a limited liability company in Nevada that is managed by Shanahan's family office. That LLC lists the same mailing address as her charitable organization, the Bia-Echo Foundation, which is named for the former couple's daughter, Echo.

While it's unclear whether Shanahan ever used the property as her primary residence, she revealed in an October 2025 interview with Frontier Magazine that she was living in a different California property: a mountaintop ranch where she was residing with her partner, Jacob Strumwasser.

Although the home was listed for rent for $175,000 a month in May, the property has now vanished from the rental market and is now available for purchase.

The listing, which is held by Michael Cunningham of Pinnacle Estate Properties, notes that it has undergone an extensive series of overhauls in recent months, describing it as a "newly completed estate.".

In a recent development, "A long, private driveway leads to a secluded sanctuary surrounded by mature trees, lush landscaping, and beautiful ocean views, with the rare privilege of keyed access to Little Dume Beach. Meticulously designed with every detail reflects an uncompromising commitment to quality and sophistication," the listing notes.

The property comes with an array of upscale features and amenities, including "keyed access to Little Dume beach," a stunning stretch of sand that is known as one of Malibu's best areas for surfing.

Recent findings suggest that the dwelling itself has plenty to offer, both inside and out. The 1.2-acre lot includes a dazzling swimming pool with a large spa and a pagoda-style area for shade.

The parcel is incredibly private, featuring a gated entrance, a long driveway, and tall trees surrounding the home.

The listing describes the home as the "epitome of 'quiet luxury,'" constructed with top-of-the-line materials and quality craftsmanship.

Upon entering the home, visitors are greeted with a spacious, airy foyer that opens to an elegant dining space and living room, where walls of windows flood the space with natural light. A curved ceiling elevates the room, while a fireplace keeps it cozy.

The dining area separates the living space from the enormous open-proposal kitchen, which features a curved island and huge French doors that open to a private deck overlooking the grounds.

For those with a fondness for entertaining, a second meal prep area with its own stove and additional appliances will no doubt prove to be one of the most-used spaces in the dwelling.

Elsewhere on the main floor are a media room—which the listing notes could be turned into an office or library—as well as a generous gym and wellness suite.

"Designed with wellness and longevity in mind, the residence incorporates advanced clean-building technologies and carefully selected materials, including a state-of-the-art VRF climate system, copper and cast-iron plumbing, rigid metal HVAC ducting, sustainable denim insulation, and specialized wiring and shielding intended to reduce EMF exposure," the description adds.

Two more bedrooms can be found on this upper level, each with its own bathroom. Another bedroom is located in a separate apartment space with a private entrance, as well as an additional kitchen and living room.

In addition to Brin, the property has a history of A-list residents, having previously been owned by pop star Pink, who purchased it for $11.9 million in 2010 and used it as her primary residence until 2016, when she sold it for $12.5 million.

The property is located just a mile away from the Malibu home Brin bought for $35 million in April 2022, just a few months after it was revealed that he and Shanahan had split.

He has since expanded his Malibu holdings with another pricier property that he picked up for $49.7 million in July 2025.

However, Brin has recently joined the growing list of billionaires pulling their fortunes out of California amid the threat of Proposition 40, a one-time, 5% wealth tax on residents worth over $1 billion—a proposal that has since been rejected.

The Google co-founder has been an outspoken critic of the tax, likening California to the Soviet Union when asked why he left the state.

Sources indicate that "I fled socialism with my family in 1979 and know the devastating, oppressive society it created in the Soviet Union. I don’t want California to end up in the same place," he told The New York Times in April.

California voters rejected Proposition 40, which would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ wealth, with most proceeds earmarked for healthcare. Opponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, argued that the measure could drive wealthy residents out of the state and reduce future tax revenue.

Brin has, quite literally, put his money where his mouth is, snapping up several properties outside of California in anticipation of the tax, including a $42 million mansion on the Nevada shore of Lake Tahoe and a $51 million Miami Beach dwelling that he bought from LVMH CEO Michael Burke at the start of the year.

The Miami property is located on the exclusive Allison Island, a 35-acre stretch of land that sits in the Biscayne Bay, between La Gorce and Miami Beach. The 24/7 guard-gated island is home to fewer than 50 single-family homes.

It was custom-built for Burke and his wife, Brigitte Burke, in 2019, five years after they purchased the 1-acre plot of land on which the home now sits for $11.7 million.

The spectacular property spans 10,000 square feet and has seven bedrooms, 8.5 bathrooms, a waterfront pool, and a private dock. The modernist design includes two separate wings of the home connected by a central walk-through area.

It's unclear whether Brin has any prepares to offload either of his Malibu homes in the wake of his move from California. Neither dwelling is right now listed on the multiple listing service.

  • Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still states Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Industry observers note that embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It states: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

Industry observers note that the schedule is fixed. Circle announced in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026.".

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide says "message limits will tighten over time until no upcoming burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

It has been revealed that circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the tech giant wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible.".

It has been revealed that funds already in transit are protected. The guide indicates "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations.".

In a recent development, the migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1.".

Sources indicate that the main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:.

Industry observers note that circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

Industry observers note that as of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle remarked "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:.

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small matter, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or upgrade integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

In a recent development, the fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:.

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

It has been revealed that for teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

Sources indicate that for everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Business knowledge workers spend their days running a gauntlet of emails, spreadsheets, messaging platforms, meetings and productivity applications, wasting hours of their time switching from one to another to get mundane tasks done.
  • Industry observers note that microsoft Corp.
  • The company’s newly introduced vision was outlined in a blog post by Microsoft Chief Marketing Officer Jared Spataro, who pointed to its comprehensive intelligence layer for work, called WorkIQ, as the critical engine behind this shift.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 00:13 EST / NOVEMBER 18 2026.

Business knowledge workers spend their days running a gauntlet of emails, spreadsheets, messaging platforms, meetings and productivity applications, wasting hours of their time switching from one to another to get mundane tasks done.

Industry observers note that microsoft Corp. is now proposing an alternative: It wants Copilot to evolve from a somewhat useful generative artificial intelligence assistant into the autonomous foundation for all business work. At Microsoft Ignite 2026 today in San Francisco, it unveiled a slate of powerful latest capabilities and features for its favorite autonomous tool as part of its ongoing effort to transform Copilot into the new workplace operating system.

The company’s newly introduced vision was outlined in a blog post by Microsoft Chief Marketing Officer Jared Spataro, who pointed to its comprehensive intelligence layer for work, called WorkIQ, as the critical engine behind this shift.

It has been revealed that spataro explained that enterprise work is notoriously messy. Microsoft 365 stores roughly 19.5 exabytes of customer’s business data, and it’s adding billions of new files, documents, emails and messages each day. For businesses, it’s not enough to just give an autonomous AI agent access to this data and expect it to start making sense of it. It needs WorkIQ, which acts as the centralized reasoning layer for all Copilot agents, retrieving data, understanding its intent, identifying what’s important for the task it has been assigned while ignoring everything else.

In a recent development, home’s key element is Auto, which is an intelligent composer that dynamically routes users’ requests and prompts to the most suitable AI model. It’s the place where most people will typically begin each upcoming task.

It has been revealed that “Tell Copilot what you want to accomplish and it intelligently routes the work to the right models and effort for the task,” Spataro explained. “For more complex work, Auto may recommend moving from Chat to Cowork. If you agree, Copilot transfers the tasks seamlessly, helping to deliver the outcome with the right level of investment.”.

Another key part of Home is called Today. It’s a “proactive command center” that’s currently available in private preview that scans a user’s email, calendar and Teams threads in order to highlight the things they have to get done that day.

Best of all, it won’t leave customers feeling overwhelmed, Spataro said, because it also helps them to complete that work. For instance, it can promptly draft replies to emails, propose alterations to someone’s schedule and queue other messages for the user to review.

Copilot’s ability to get work done has been advanced by its deeper integration with Microsoft’s Office suite. Spataro said the firm is bringing the full capabilities of Office directly into the Copilot application.

According to recent reports, as a result, users will be able to move effortlessly from ideation on a notepad or whiteboard to conjure up a completed Word document or Excel spreadsheet based on what they just outlined. Those files will live entirely within Copilot, which gains the ability to co-author alongside human colleagues. Because Office is now native to Copilot, every document and file will be secured by Microsoft 365’s strict security and compliance controls, Spataro mentioned.

According to recent reports, human-to-agent collaboration is being boosted too with the arrival of Copilot Workspaces, which is a kind of canvas that both can access, Spataro said. Within Copilot Workspaces, an agent might draft a section of a document, then notify a human to come and review it when they get the chance. The human will be able to leave comments for other agents to address.

Recent findings suggest that autopilot is very different from standard AI agents that are programmed to wait for a user’s prompts. It’s continuously available, watching various Teams channels and the user’s email inbox for updates. It can automate recurring work processes, and it can manage entire project pipelines, such as a multistep supplier review, fully autonomously, Spataro said.

Autopilot is powerful, but safeguards are in place. Information technology teams have complete control over what it can and can’t access, and if something goes wrong they can step in and block it from doing anything else at a moment’s notice.

“Its sign-ins and actions are logged under its own name, so security teams have a clear audit trail,” Spataro explained. “Powered by WorkIQ, it understands how your organization works within existing permissions. You decide what work Autopilot takes on and it will always check with you before key actions.”.

Industry observers note that coding continues to be a major focus, and now Microsoft is giving everyday knowledge workers the ability to build software that can help them get their work done even faster. With Copilot Code, launching in a few week’s time, customers will be able to generate interactive dashboards, persistent desktop widgets and lightweight business applications from simple, natural language prompts.

All of these Copilot-generated apps will be hosted within Copilot Managed Runtime, which is a newly introduced, highly-secure environment that IT teams can monitor to ensure none of them pose a risk to the company’s data.

It has been revealed that to reassure organizations that their AI agents are not only secure, but also providing real value, Microsoft has updated the Agent 365 platform to give teams more control and visibility into their AI spending. Agent 365 now comes with a Business Analytics feature that brings a FinOps-style approach to AI budgeting.

In a recent development, whereas most platforms just track token consumption, it goes further, measuring each agent’s return on investment by looking at the “work completed” and the number of hours it took. According to Spataro, this will give companies a much clearer picture of the benefits of their AI investments.

In a recent development, finally, there’s a lot going on in terms of business data connectivity. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • For many Americans these days, affordable housing is still out of reach.
  • Airbnb is stepping up to the plate to try to change that.
  • Recent findings suggest that the company declared a $1 million annual Housing Innovation Prize to support innovators and entrepreneurs who are striving to make it faster, easier, and cheaper to buy homes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For many Americans these days, affordable housing is still out of reach.

Airbnb is stepping up to the plate to try to change that.

Recent findings suggest that the company declared a $1 million annual Housing Innovation Prize to support innovators and entrepreneurs who are striving to make it faster, easier, and cheaper to buy homes. It plans to distribute one award per year over a five-year period.

The $1 million prizes are intended for U.S.-based companies and nonprofits with ideas that are already in the works but need funding to succeed. These may include factory-built homes, faster construction sides, expedited permitting, or easier financing for new homes.

Recent findings suggest that “Airbnb started as a way to help my co-founders pay their rent. Today millions of people do the same. Now we are helping to finance the building of housing in communities nationwide. We want to encourage others, through this prize, to think more creatively and ambitiously about home building and delivering affordability. Necessity is the mother of invention,” mentioned Nathan Blecharczyk, Airbnb’s co-founder and chief strategy officer, in a recent press release.

While Airbnb’s efforts are a step in the right direction, experts agree that addressing the affordability crisis as a whole requires more funding, innovation, and collaboration across the industry.

Airbnb's initiative brings renewed attention to the need for more housing in the U.S., and finding ways to build it more efficiently and affordably is becoming increasingly crucial.

Realtor.com® data highlights how serious the housing supply gap has become.

According to recent reports, in 2025, latest-home construction fell short of household formations, pushing the U.S. housing supply gap to an estimated 4.03 million homes. This demonstrates the need for new solutions that can make it easier and more efficient to build homes.

Addressing the shortage will also require evaluating and changing policies and regulations that may slow down construction and raise costs. That’s where the Realtor.com Let America Build initiative comes in.

It strives to encourage discussions and solutions on the U.S. home inventory and affordability crisis.

Several factors are slowing down homebuilding and driving up construction costs in the U.S., and initiatives like Airbnb’s could help.

“Builders cite slow permit processes, increased material expenses, and lack of skilled labor as the main factors raising construction costs,” says Michael Pearson, senior vice president of business development at A&D Mortgage LLC in Ft. Lauderdale, FL.

Additionally, with expenses on the rise and the pressure to keep homes marketable and affordable, margins for contractors and developers are very low.

Innovations for factory-built or modular homes, for example, could improve the situation. These homes are traditionally built homes assembled off site and delivered to a plot of land.

Recent findings suggest that “While modular homes are more economical, as you don’t have to ship supplies and workers to a site build and you can better control costs and material overages, they come with logistical concerns, primarily getting the modular home on site. Innovation may find a solution that so far has not shown itself,” adds Pearson.

Gay Cororaton, chief economist at MIAMI Realtors + RWorld in Miami, points out that modular homes are simply more attainable for more households.

Recent findings suggest that “The average price of a new manufactured home is less than $150,000, which could go up to, say, $300,000 for a double-wide home. At today's mortgage rates, for a household with $100,000 in income, that’s more affordable than a traditional home,” Cororaton explains.

According to recent reports, still, while the Airbnb Housing Innovation Prize could turn promising ideas into realities, Pearson believes $1 million prizes won’t be enough and innovations must be part of a greater strategy where we highlight issues, communicate ideas, and have demonstrable progress. It’s also notable for other organizations to jump on board.

Industry observers note that “I’d like to see more companies, nonprofits, and government agencies get involved with this kind of action. Housing safety and affordability is this issue of this generation, and together we can find solutions,” states Pearson.

Robert Trent, CEO and principal at Builders Capital in Puyallup, WA, agrees with Pearson and believes the success of Airbnb’s initiative will depend on what gets built after the award.

“The best-case scenario is quality homes people can afford, delivered at a lower total cost, with results that can be replicated across different communities,” Trent adds.

Tech Report: Wisconsin Couple Seek To Enforce $1,350 Judgment Against Each of Their Neighbors in HOA Dispute

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A neighborhood outside Green Bay, WI, is locked in a yearslong legal battle, as one couple is now taking legal action against their neighbors to collect a $200,000 settlement.
  • What began as a dispute over a backyard fence has turned into an ongoing series of lawsuits, with neighbors being forced to pay $1,350 each in a settlement—and those who haven’t are now being taken to court.
  • Industry observers note that the case is centered around Michael and Lisa Newman and their five children, who reside in the Nazcr Trac neighborhood in De Pere, WI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A neighborhood outside Green Bay, WI, is locked in a yearslong legal battle, as one couple is now taking legal action against their neighbors to collect a $200,000 settlement.

What began as a dispute over a backyard fence has turned into an ongoing series of lawsuits, with neighbors being forced to pay $1,350 each in a settlement—and those who haven’t are now being taken to court.

Industry observers note that the case is centered around Michael and Lisa Newman and their five children, who reside in the Nazcr Trac neighborhood in De Pere, WI. After some of their children were diagnosed with autism, the Newmans wanted to build a fence around their backyard, as they wanted the children to be able to play outside safely.

Citing the children’s diagnoses and that two of their children “demonstrated significant risk of elopement,” according to a press release from the Metropolitan Milwaukee Fair Housing Council, the Newmans wrote to the Nazcr Trac Property Owners Association (NTPOA) to request an accommodation to the subdivision’s “no fence” rule.

Neither the initial request, sent in July 2019, nor a subsequent request in December 2020, which included information about the association’s legal obligation to consider an accommodation due to the children’s disabilities, were answered by the association.

In a recent development, in August 2021, the Newmans filed a lawsuit against the association in federal court, alleging that it had discriminated based on disability, a violation of the Fair Housing Amendments Act. A judge granted a preliminary injunction in May 2022 that prohibits the NTPOA from enforcing the rule, and the family built their fence in time for summer, three years after the initial request.

While the family got their wish, the battle was just beginning for other residents of Nazcr Trac.

In August 2024, a settlement was reached, requiring the NTPOA to pay the Newmans $200,000—a payment that would be passed on directly to each household in the association.

Following the settlement, each property in the neighborhood was looking at a $1,350 bill. Residents told WGBA that they were frustrated by the situation and many had been unaware of the dispute until they received the charge.

One anonymous resident told the local station that most residents would have had no matter with the fence, and a poll of members could have saved a lot of time and money.

“If the board had polled us as members, a large amount of the members would have said, 'Absolutely, let the family do what they need to do to take care of their family,’” the resident said during WGBA’s initial coverage in 2025.

At the time, Lisa Newman told the station that she felt “not great” about her neighbors being on the hook for the settlement payment.

“It's just a really unfortunate situation, I think, for everybody involved, and the board kind of made that decision for everybody,” she told WGBA.

However, in September, the Newmans filed a new lawsuit against the NTPOA and a number of homeowners who still owe on the settlement.

Sources indicate that sixty-nine homeowners settled following the initial lawsuit, the Newmans’ attorney, Victoria Davis Dávila, told WGBA. The rest are now facing legal troubles of their own.

In a recent development, “There’s an outstanding judgment," Davis Dávila told WGBA. "You had the opportunity to pay. You chose not to pay it.".

In addition to the association, 33 residents are named in the newly introduced filing.

“The Newmans want just as bad as anybody else to put this behind them,” Davis Dávila said, adding that the NTPOA membership as a whole could potentially be held liable if the outstanding amount isn’t paid.

The latest lawsuit is frustrating and stressful for many homeowners who thought the matter would be behind them by now.

“Why is this coming back to us? It’s so unfair,” an anonymous homeowners told WGBA.

An answer and affirmative defense was filed by the Property Owner’s Association on Nov. 16, but the contents of the document were not publicly available at the time of publication.

Realtor.com® reached out to the legal counsel of both the association and the Newmans, but received no response.

Bitcoin price is struggling to find direction just below $65,000 as we brace for Nvidia earnings report. BTC USD has recovered from its weekend low near $62,000, but remains down 13% over seven days. Its modest rebound comes as technology stocks face yet another selling pressure.

It has been revealed that this timing puts the Bitcoin price in an uncomfortable position. Nvidia’s results could determine if investors return to risk assets or abandon another crowded trade. With market sentiment still deep in extreme fear, we still have little conviction that the worst is over.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, Michael Burry is increasing his bearish bets against technology stocks. The investor made famous by The Major Short is targeting the Nasdaq-100 and semiconductor sector. His positioning raises an ugly question: Is the AI boom approaching its own dot-com moment?

Industry observers note that burry doubled his Nasdaq-100 put position on November 12, targeting early 2027 options 20% below the index’s market level. He also bought back part of his previously reduced bearish position in the VanEck Semiconductor ETF.

Recent findings suggest that his argument goes beyond stretched stock valuations. Burry believes conventional accounting earnings can exaggerate technology companies’ underlying profitability. Depreciation schedules, particularly across expensive data-center infrastructure, sit at the center of his concerns.

Consider a hyperscaler investing billions in GPUs and AI infrastructure. Those purchases become capital assets rather than immediate operating expenses. Companies subsequently recognize depreciation across their estimated useful lives.

Recent findings suggest that this accounting treatment can make current earnings look stronger than the underlying cash economics. If hardware becomes obsolete faster than expected, reported profitability could overstate actual investment returns.

It has been revealed that the concern becomes significant when companies must continuously replace expensive accelerators. Their infrastructure spending needs to generate sufficient revenue before the equipment loses economic value.

In a recent development, burry isn’t alone in questioning the investment cycle. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman previously acknowledged excessive enthusiasm surrounding artificial intelligence.

Sources indicate that “Are we in a phase where investors as a whole are overexcited about AI? My opinion is yes,” Altman remarked.

Jeff Bezos offered another interpretation, describing the spending cycle as an “industrial bubble.” He argued that excessive investment could still produce valuable infrastructure, even when individual investors lose money.

Nvidia’s own Jensen Huang previously defended the industry’s economics. According to him, the AI infrastructure was already generating productive revenue, rather than merely attracting speculative capital.

Industry observers note that the disagreement exposes the central tension surrounding the AI bubble. Demand can be genuine while valuations and infrastructure commitments become unsustainable.

The dot-com crash offers an vital historical comparison. The Nasdaq Composite lost 78% between March 2000 and October 2002. Internet technology survived, but countless businesses and investors did not.

Recent findings suggest that today’s AI infrastructure market has similarities, particularly aggressive capital expenditure and expectations of exponential demand. However, established hyperscalers now finance much of the expansion through enormous operating businesses.

Now, can future AI revenue justify today’s investment?

Industry observers note that bitcoin once traded with relatively little correlation to traditional equities. That relationship changed dramatically as institutional participation expanded.

In a recent development, CME Group’s historical correlation research illustrates the shift. Between 2014 and 2016, Bitcoin’s correlation with the S&P 500 stood near -0.01. Its correlation with the Nasdaq-100 was effectively zero. Between 2020 and 2022, those correlations climbed to 0.40 and 0.42, respectively. They remained positive through April 2025, reaching 0.30 against both indices.

It has been revealed that the shift matters because institutional investors increasingly treat Bitcoin as another liquid risk asset. Portfolio rebalancing, leveraged positions, and macroeconomic conditions can influence its price alongside technology stocks.

In a recent development, an AI sell-off could create another liquidity shock across crypto. Investors facing losses elsewhere might sell Bitcoin to raise cash or reduce overall exposure. But an AI correction doesn’t automatically invalidate Bitcoin’s monetary thesis. A technology valuation reset could eventually redirect capital toward alternative assets.

The gap lies between an isolated technology correction and a financial liquidity crisis. Bitcoin could eventually decouple from semiconductor stocks under the first scenario. The second could pressure both markets simultaneously. For now, Bitcoin price remains exposed to the same risk appetite driving technology shares.

According to recent reports, nvidia’s third-quarter fiscal 2027 results arrive at a particularly sensitive moment. Wall Street expects $109 billion in revenue and $2.47 in adjusted earnings per share.

It has been revealed that investors will focus heavily on Data Center revenue, gross margins, and forward guidance. The manufacturer’s Vera Rubin platform also faces scrutiny as customers expand their AI infrastructure commitments.

Sources indicate that A headline earnings beat might not satisfy investors demanding another acceleration in growth. Strong revenue accompanied by cautious guidance could trigger another sell-the-news reaction.

The opposite scenario could restore confidence across technology stocks. Strong guidance would reinforce expectations that hyperscaler spending remains sustainable. Bitcoin could benefit if investors regain their appetite for speculative assets.

Technically, Bitcoin needs to stabilize above its recent $62,000 weekend low. A break below that level would expose the psychologically important $60,000 threshold.

A stronger recovery would put $68,000 back into view as an crucial technical resistance area. Reclaiming that level could help establish if buyers are returning.

Bitcoin price now faces a test extending beyond crypto markets. Nvidia must demonstrate that AI infrastructure spending can translate into durable earnings growth.

Burry is betting that expectations have run too far ahead. Huang’s former firm built the infrastructure powering the AI revolution, but investors now need proof of its economic returns.

If the AI bubble starts deflating, Bitcoin must answer another question: Can it survive without Wall Street’s appetite for technology risk?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the XRP Ledger (XRPL) will be delivering a major patch on Dec. 3, which will address the occasional sluggishness the blockchain network has been experiencing in recent weeks.

As stated in a recent XRP Ledger Operations announcement, the network will be rolling out its new version 3.5.0, which will exclusively include technical improvements and bug fixes, such as a lasting fix for the relatively slow ledger closing times.

"XRPL version 3.5.0 will be on Dec 3. Just improvements/fixes, including a long-lasting fix for the occasional slow ledger close times," XRP Ledger Operations noted.

The developers have informed customers that the interim fixes to help improve the situation have already been working effectively.

"Interim fixes already helped improve close times, and we are watching the network very closely," it added.

This is a critical advancement in improving the reliability of the XRP Ledger, a network widely used to process cryptocurrency payments, tokenization, and stablecoin transactions.

The latest improvement to the XRPL comes after the blockchain network suffered technical issues in October, when some ledgers were closing much slower than usual.

Industry observers note that the XRP Ledger usually closes new ledgers once every three to five seconds. This ensures that transaction confirmations happen fairly swiftly.

However, intermittent sluggishness was seen on the network, as XRP Ledger Operations admitted on Oct. 21. The team later confirmed that its developers were already working on the concern.

Afterward, XRP Ledger Operations started sharing a recommended configuration update for xrpld software with network operators such as validators and other infrastructure providers.

The temporary fixes were helpful. On Oct. 22, XRP Ledger Operations shared that the occasional slower ledger closures were no longer happening, thanks to the newly introduced recommended configuration.

That mentioned, the developers remain hard at work to deliver a software fix that will correct the concern once and for all, a long-term solution that would not rely solely on temporary changes.

That is why the December release is expected to finally bring that permanent fix.

In the meantime, Vet, one of the notable XRP Ledger validators, has already assured the community that the blockchain network is always being monitored as developers work on more improvements.

In a recent post on X, he stressed that a great amount of work has been put into network monitoring, information security and engineering.

Vet said that their engineers are always on call to address any possible incidents.
